disease.name: Bronchitis
disease.scientific_name: Bronchitis — Acute Tracheobronchitis / Chronic Bronchitis / Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Bronchitis (AECB)
disease.icd_10_code: J20 (Acute bronchitis); J20.0 (Acute bronchitis due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae); J20.7 (Acute bronchitis due to Echovirus); J20.9 (Acute bronchitis, unspecified); J41.0 (Simple chronic bronchitis); J41.1 (Mucopurulent chronic bronchitis); J42 (Unspecified chronic bronchitis); J44.1 (COPD with acute exacerbation); J44.0 (COPD with acute lower respiratory infection); A37 (Whooping cough — Bordetella pertussis); J21 (Acute bronchiolitis — children)
disease.category: Respiratory Disease / Infectious Disease / Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

overview.description: Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes — the large and medium-calibre airways (bronchi and bronchioles) that conduct air from the trachea into the lung parenchyma. Inflammation causes swelling of the bronchial mucosa, increased mucus secretion, and narrowing of the airway lumen, resulting in the hallmark symptom of a productive (mucus-producing) cough. Bronchitis exists in two clinically and aetiologically distinct forms: (1) Acute bronchitis — a self-limiting, almost always viral respiratory infection causing cough lasting 1-3 weeks; accounting for approximately 5-10% of all primary care consultations and one of the most common reasons for antibiotic prescribing (despite the majority of cases not requiring antibiotics — one of the greatest drivers of global antibiotic resistance); and (2) Chronic bronchitis — a component of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), defined clinically as a productive cough persisting for at least 3 months in each of two consecutive years, caused by progressive irreversible airway inflammation from tobacco smoke, indoor air pollution (biomass fuel combustion — a massive cause in India), and occupational exposures. A third important clinical scenario is acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (AECB) — a sudden worsening of cough, sputum, and breathlessness in a patient with established chronic bronchitis or COPD, which can be life-threatening in advanced disease.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the bronchial tubes (bronchi and bronchioles — the conducting airways); in chronic and severe acute disease: lung parenchyma, pulmonary vasculature, and right ventricle (cor pulmonale in advanced COPD)
overview.prevalence: Acute bronchitis: one of the most common illnesses globally — approximately 44 million cases per year in the USA alone; accounts for 2.5-5% of all primary care consultations; most common reason for inappropriate antibiotic prescribing. Chronic bronchitis: affects approximately 9% of adults globally; component of COPD which affects 251 million people worldwide and is the third leading cause of death globally. In India: COPD affects an estimated 55 million people; biomass fuel combustion (chulha cooking — open wood, dung, crop fires) is the leading cause in non-smokers, particularly rural women.
overview.age_group: Acute bronchitis: all ages, peak in children and young adults; Chronic bronchitis: predominantly adults over 40 years with smoking or pollution exposure; AECB: adults with established COPD
overview.is_contagious_note: Acute viral bronchitis is contagious — the causative viruses (influenza, rhinovirus, RSV, etc.) spread by respiratory droplets, aerosols, and contact with contaminated surfaces. Chronic bronchitis itself is not infectious but exacerbations triggered by respiratory infections can be contagious.
overview.is_curable_note: Acute bronchitis is self-limiting and resolves completely. Chronic bronchitis (COPD) is not curable but progression can be dramatically slowed or halted with smoking cessation and other interventions; lung function lost to COPD is not fully recoverable.
overview.is_chronic_note: Acute bronchitis is not chronic (resolves in 1-3 weeks). Chronic bronchitis is by definition chronic — a lifelong condition requiring ongoing management.
overview.key_fact: Over 90% of acute bronchitis cases are caused by viruses and do NOT require antibiotics — inappropriate antibiotic prescribing for bronchitis is one of the largest drivers of antibiotic resistance globally. For chronic bronchitis: stopping smoking at any age is the single most effective intervention — no medication comes close to the benefit of smoking cessation in preserving lung function.

types.name: Acute Viral Bronchitis
types.description: The most common form — responsible for approximately 90-95% of all acute bronchitis cases. Caused by respiratory viruses infecting the bronchial mucosa, causing inflammatory oedema, mucus hypersecretion, and temporary impairment of mucociliary clearance. Acute viral bronchitis is a self-limiting illness — the immune system clears the infection without antibiotics in the vast majority of healthy individuals within 1-3 weeks. The key public health challenge is that patients and clinicians often equate purulent (yellow-green) sputum with bacterial infection requiring antibiotics — this is incorrect; purulent sputum in acute viral bronchitis reflects the normal inflammatory response (neutrophil-derived peroxidases colouring the mucus), NOT bacterial infection.

major_causative_viruses.proportion: 30-40% — most common cause of acute viral bronchitis
major_causative_viruses.features: Causes the common cold as primary syndrome; can descend to lower respiratory tract causing bronchitis; peaks September-October and April-May; over 100 serotypes — no vaccine possible

major_causative_viruses.proportion: 20-30% — particularly November to March (temperate climates); all year round in India
major_causative_viruses.features: More severe systemic illness than rhinovirus (higher fever, myalgia, malaise — distinguishes influenza from common cold); bronchitis is a common lower respiratory component of influenza; can progress to influenza pneumonia; antiviral treatment (oseltamivir) beneficial within 48 hours
major_causative_viruses.severity: Moderate to Severe — higher risk of complications (pneumonia, respiratory failure) in elderly, COPD, pregnancy, immunocompromised

major_causative_viruses.proportion: 10-20% in adults; dominant cause of bronchiolitis in infants
major_causative_viruses.features: Major cause of hospitalisation in infants under 2 years (bronchiolitis — distinct from adult bronchitis); in adults causes bronchitis indistinguishable from other viral bronchitis; RSV vaccines and monoclonal antibodies (nirsevimab) now available for high-risk infants and elderly
major_causative_viruses.severity: Mild in healthy adults; severe in infants, elderly, COPD, immunocompromised

major_causative_viruses.features: Causes croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) in children — barking cough, stridor; acute bronchitis in adults; seasonal peaks
major_causative_viruses.severity: Usually mild in adults; croup can be severe in young children

major_causative_viruses.proportion: Common coronaviruses 229E, OC43, HKU1, NL63 cause ~15% of common colds and bronchitis; SARS-CoV-2 important since 2020
major_causative_viruses.features: Common coronaviruses: mild bronchitis syndrome; SARS-CoV-2: acute bronchitis may be the presenting syndrome; persistent cough can last weeks post-COVID
major_causative_viruses.severity: Common coronaviruses: mild; SARS-CoV-2: highly variable from mild bronchitis to critical pneumonia

major_causative_viruses.features: Closely related to RSV; peaks in late winter/early spring; causes bronchitis, bronchiolitis (infants), and pneumonia; important but underrecognised pathogen
Can cause prolonged and more severe bronchitis; associated with outbreaks in military recruits; conjunctivitis may coexist (pharyngoconjunctival fever)

types.prognosis: Excellent — spontaneous resolution in 1-3 weeks in otherwise healthy individuals; 50% of patients still have a cough at 3 weeks (normal); 25% at 4 weeks (normal variant); antibiotics shorten duration by only 6-12 hours but cause significant side effects and resistance

types.name: Acute Bacterial Bronchitis
types.description: A minority (5-10%) of acute bronchitis cases are caused by bacteria. Importantly, the bacteria causing acute bronchitis are primarily 'atypical' bacteria (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Bordetella) rather than the classical pyogenic bacteria causing pneumonia. These atypical organisms are intracellular or have thin cell walls — they are intrinsically resistant to penicillin and amoxicillin but respond to macrolides and tetracyclines. Bordetella pertussis (whooping cough) is a particularly important bacterial cause that is frequently missed and requires specific antibiotic treatment and public health notification.

major_causative_bacteria.proportion: Important cause of prolonged cough (>2-3 weeks) — often missed in adults; responsible for 1-6% of adult cough lasting >2 weeks
major_causative_bacteria.features: Classic whooping cough (paroxysmal cough followed by characteristic 'whoop' inspiratory sound) is most obvious in children; adults often present with just persistent cough without the classic whoop; post-tussive vomiting (vomiting after coughing fits) is characteristic; cough can last 6-10 weeks ('100-day cough'); lymphocytosis on FBC; apnoea in infants (can be fatal)
major_causative_bacteria.diagnosis: Nasopharyngeal PCR swab (most sensitive); Bordetella serology (IgG) for cases presenting >3 weeks; FBC showing lymphocytosis
major_causative_bacteria.treatment: Azithromycin 500mg daily for 5 days (first-line); erythromycin 500mg four times daily for 14 days (alternative); clarithromycin; antibiotics reduce transmission but may not shorten duration if started >3 weeks after onset
major_causative_bacteria.public_health: NOTIFIABLE DISEASE in most countries including India — must be reported to public health authority; contact tracing and prophylaxis for household contacts; exclude from nursery/school until 5 days of antibiotics completed

major_causative_bacteria.proportion: 5-15% of acute bronchitis; epidemic cycles every 3-5 years; more common in school-age children and young adults
major_causative_bacteria.features: Gradual onset (unlike viral bronchitis); persistent dry then productive cough; low-grade fever; headache; sore throat preceding cough; bullous myringitis (fluid-filled blisters on eardrum — pathognomonic); extrapulmonary manifestations: haemolytic anaemia (cold agglutinins), skin rash (erythema multiforme), neurological complications; may progress to atypical pneumonia
major_causative_bacteria.diagnosis: Mycoplasma IgM serology; PCR (nasopharyngeal swab or sputum); cold agglutinins (non-specific)
major_causative_bacteria.treatment: Azithromycin 500mg daily for 5 days (first-line); doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 7-14 days; clarithromycin; NOT amoxicillin or cephalosporins (no cell wall — intrinsic resistance)

major_causative_bacteria.proportion: 5-10% of acute bronchitis and community-acquired pneumonia
major_causative_bacteria.features: Gradual onset; persistent dry cough; pharyngitis; often slow progression; can progress to pneumonia; difficult to distinguish clinically from Mycoplasma
major_causative_bacteria.diagnosis: Serology (IgM, IgG); PCR; difficult to culture
major_causative_bacteria.treatment: Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 10-14 days; azithromycin; fluoroquinolones

major_causative_bacteria.proportion: Less common than B. pertussis; similar clinical picture but milder
major_causative_bacteria.features: Similar cough syndrome to whooping cough; not prevented by pertussis vaccine; treat same as pertussis
major_causative_bacteria.note: Not covered by standard whooping cough vaccine

types.important_note: Secondary bacterial bronchitis can follow viral upper respiratory tract infection — 'superinfection'; the virus damages bronchial epithelium and mucociliary defences, allowing bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) to colonise. However, this is less common than previously believed — purulent sputum alone is NOT sufficient to diagnose bacterial superinfection.

types.name: Chronic Bronchitis
types.description: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a productive cough persisting for at least 3 months per year in each of two consecutive years, not explained by another cause. It is the major component of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) along with emphysema (destruction of alveolar walls). Chronic bronchitis results from years of bronchial mucosal irritation from cigarette smoke, indoor air pollution (biomass fuel smoke from wood-burning chulhas — an enormous problem in India), outdoor air pollution, occupational dusts and fumes, and recurrent respiratory infections. The pathological hallmarks are: mucous gland hypertrophy and hyperplasia (Reid index >0.4 — ratio of mucous gland thickness to bronchial wall thickness); goblet cell hyperplasia; chronic inflammatory infiltrate; airway wall thickening; and progressive, largely irreversible airflow obstruction.
types.epidemiology: Affects approximately 9% of adults globally; 55 million people in India; more common in men (historically due to higher smoking rates) but increasing in Indian women from biomass fuel exposure; predominantly in adults over 40 years with cumulative smoke exposure; 90% of COPD cases attributable to tobacco in high-income countries but 50% in India from biomass fuel
types.definition: Productive cough ≥3 months per year for ≥2 consecutive years; confirmed airflow obstruction on spirometry (FEV1/FVC ratio post-bronchodilator <0.7 = COPD); FEV1% predicted determines GOLD severity (I-IV)

gold_classification.symptoms: Mild symptoms; chronic cough with sputum
Worsening dyspnoea; reduced exercise tolerance; exacerbations
Severe dyspnoea; significantly impaired quality of life; life-threatening exacerbations; possible respiratory failure

types.causes_and_risk_factors: Cigarette smoking (most common globally — dose-dependent; 15-20 pack-years typically needed); bidis (Indian hand-rolled cigarettes — contain unfiltered tobacco — higher carcinogen concentration; more harmful per cigarette than manufactured cigarettes; major COPD driver in India); hookah/shisha pipe smoking; biomass fuel combustion (wood, dung, crop residue — 3 billion people globally cook on open fires; smoke equivalent to smoking several cigarettes per day; leading cause of COPD in non-smoking Indian rural women); occupational exposure (coal dust — miners; silica — quarry workers; cadmium; grain dust; isocyanates); outdoor air pollution (high PM2.5 — major Indian cities have among the world's worst air quality); childhood respiratory infections (permanent airway remodelling); alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (genetic cause of early-onset COPD)
types.prognosis: Progressive and irreversible unless cause removed; 10-15-year reduction in life expectancy with severe COPD; smoking cessation at any stage significantly slows progression; pulmonary rehabilitation improves quality of life and reduces hospitalisations

types.name: Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Bronchitis (AECB) / COPD Exacerbation (AECOPD)
types.description: An acute worsening of respiratory symptoms in a patient with established chronic bronchitis or COPD — beyond normal day-to-day variation — requiring a change in regular medication. AECB is the most common cause of emergency hospitalisation in patients with COPD and a major cause of COPD-related mortality. Exacerbations accelerate the progressive decline in lung function and quality of life in COPD patients. Approximately 50-70% of AECB episodes are triggered by respiratory infections (viral in 50%, bacterial in 25-30%, mixed in 20-25%); remaining exacerbations are triggered by air pollution, cardiac events, or have no identifiable cause.
triggers: Respiratory viral infections — rhinovirus (most common), influenza, RSV, coronavirus
Bacterial infections — Haemophilus influenzae (most common), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (in severe COPD/FEV1 <30%)
Air pollution events — high PM2.5, ozone, nitrogen dioxide
Cardiac decompensation (heart failure exacerbating respiratory symptoms)
Pulmonary embolism — must be excluded in AECB not responding to standard treatment
Pneumothorax — spontaneous or related to bullous emphysema

criteria: Increased sputum purulence (change to yellow-green colour)
anthonisen_criteria.type_I: All 3 criteria present — high likelihood of bacterial trigger — most likely to benefit from antibiotics
anthonisen_criteria.type_II: 2 of 3 criteria present — moderate likelihood of bacterial trigger
anthonisen_criteria.type_III: 1 criterion plus at least 1 of: URTI symptoms within 5 days; fever without other cause; increased wheeze; increased cough — possible bacterial trigger

types.severity_assessment: CURB-65-like scoring not validated for AECB; hospitalisation decision based on: oxygen saturation <92%, arterial blood gas (hypoxia, hypercapnia — type 2 respiratory failure), respiratory rate >25, use of accessory muscles, altered consciousness, inability to manage at home, inadequate social support

types.name: Allergic and Eosinophilic Bronchitis
types.description: Bronchial inflammation driven by allergic (IgE-mediated) or eosinophilic mechanisms rather than infection or smoking. Includes: (1) Asthmatic bronchitis — overlapping features of asthma and bronchitis; bronchial hyperresponsiveness with episodic wheeze, cough, and inflammation; (2) Non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis (NAEB) — chronic cough with sputum eosinophilia (>3% eosinophils on induced sputum), no bronchial hyperresponsiveness (unlike asthma), no variable airflow obstruction; responds dramatically to inhaled corticosteroids; important cause of unexplained chronic cough; (3) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) — hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus in asthmatic and cystic fibrosis patients.
types.features: NAEB: chronic dry cough often the only symptom; induced sputum eosinophilia; responds to ICS; important differential for chronic cough. Asthmatic bronchitis: reversible bronchospasm on spirometry; responds to bronchodilators and ICS.
types.management: Inhaled corticosteroids (budesonide, beclomethasone); identify and remove allergen; oral prednisolone for severe episodes

types.name: Occupational and Chemical Bronchitis
types.description: Bronchial inflammation caused by chronic inhalation of occupational dusts, chemical fumes, gases, and vapours. Distinct from smoking-related chronic bronchitis by occupational history and temporal relationship to workplace exposure. Key occupational causes: coal dust (coal workers' pneumoconiosis + bronchitis); silica dust (quarry, mine, construction workers); cadmium fumes (battery manufacture); isocyanates (spray painting, foam manufacture — also causes asthma); grain dust and mould (farmers' lung — hypersensitivity pneumonitis); welding fumes; nitrogen oxides; chlorine and ammonia gas. In India: coal mines in Jharkhand and Odisha; cotton textile (byssinosis — Monday fever pattern, cough worse at start of work week); brick kilns.
types.diagnosis: Occupational history is paramount; lung function testing (spirometry, diffusion capacity); high-resolution CT; bronchoalveolar lavage; specific inhalation challenge testing
types.management: Remove from exposure (most important — like smoking cessation); respiratory protective equipment; legal obligations under occupational health law; inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids for symptom management; workers' compensation assessment

severity_levels.name: Mild Acute Bronchitis
severity_levels.description: Self-limiting viral bronchitis in an otherwise healthy adult with no underlying respiratory disease. The vast majority of community acute bronchitis cases.
severity_levels.criteria: Productive or non-productive cough; low-grade fever (<38.5°C) or no fever; mild fatigue; no significant breathlessness at rest; no oxygen impairment; oxygen saturation >96%; no signs of pneumonia; no underlying COPD or asthma; able to manage at home
severity_levels.functional_impact: Uncomfortable; cough may disturb sleep; able to continue most activities; sick leave 3-7 days
severity_levels.management: Self-care at home; adequate fluid intake (minimum 2L/day); honey and ginger for cough; steam inhalation; paracetamol for fever and discomfort; no antibiotics required in healthy adults; reassure regarding expected duration (cough up to 3 weeks is normal in viral bronchitis); return to work when fever-free and feeling able
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Fever >38.5°C; increased breathlessness; oxygen saturation falling; not improving after 10-14 days; cough becoming significantly worse; known COPD or asthma

severity_levels.name: Moderate Acute Bronchitis or Mild AECB
severity_levels.description: Acute bronchitis with significant systemic illness or breathlessness, or mild-moderate exacerbation of chronic bronchitis/COPD with manageable symptoms at home or in primary care.
severity_levels.criteria: Fever 38.5-39.5°C; significant productive cough with purulent sputum; moderate breathlessness (dyspnoea on exertion or walking); wheeze; heart rate 100-110 bpm; oxygen saturation 92-96%; known COPD with worsening symptoms (GOLD II-III, Anthonisen Type I or II); increased use of rescue bronchodilator
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significantly impairs daily function; reduced exercise tolerance; unable to work; disrupted sleep from cough
severity_levels.management: GP or urgent care assessment; spirometry if COPD suspected; chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia; sputum culture if purulent; bronchodilator (salbutamol inhaler or nebuliser); prednisolone oral 30-40 mg for 5 days (AECB); antibiotics if Anthonisen Type I or II criteria met, or bacterial cause suspected (atypical organisms); adequate hydration; mucolytics; review in 48-72 hours
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Oxygen saturation falling <92%; inability to manage at home; respiratory rate >25; altered consciousness; severe underlying COPD (GOLD IV)

severity_levels.name: Severe AECB / Acute-on-Chronic Respiratory Failure
severity_levels.description: Severe exacerbation of COPD/chronic bronchitis with significant hypoxia or hypercapnia requiring hospitalisation and advanced respiratory support.
severity_levels.criteria: Oxygen saturation <92% on air; respiratory rate >25 breaths/min; PaO2 <8 kPa (60 mmHg) on arterial blood gas; PaCO2 >6 kPa (45 mmHg — type 2 respiratory failure / hypercapnic failure); use of accessory muscles of respiration (sternocleidomastoid, intercostal recession); paradoxical breathing; confusion or drowsiness (CO2 narcosis); tachycardia >110 bpm; cyanosis (peripheral or central); pH <7.35 on ABG (respiratory acidosis)
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to complete sentences; unable to stand or walk; complete incapacitation; requires hospital level care
severity_levels.management: Hospital admission; controlled oxygen therapy (target SpO2 88-92% in COPD — avoid hyperoxia causing CO2 retention); nebulised bronchodilators (salbutamol + ipratropium); systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 30-40 mg oral or hydrocortisone IV); IV antibiotics; arterial blood gas monitoring; ECG; non-invasive ventilation (NIV — BiPAP) for pH <7.35 with hypercapnia; physiotherapy for secretion clearance; VTE prophylaxis; close observation for deterioration
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: NIV failure; pH <7.25; respiratory arrest or imminent arrest; haemodynamic collapse

severity_levels.name: Critical / Respiratory Failure Requiring Mechanical Ventilation
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening respiratory failure from severe AECB requiring invasive mechanical ventilation in ICU, or acute bronchitis causing respiratory failure in immunocompromised or severely unwell patients.
severity_levels.criteria: Respiratory arrest or near-arrest; failure of NIV (unable to maintain pH >7.25, oxygen or consciousness deteriorating); pH <7.25 on NIV; haemodynamic collapse; Glasgow Coma Score <8; inability to protect airway
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation; lung-protective ventilation strategy; deep sedation and paralysis if required; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; maximal bronchodilator therapy; haemodynamic monitoring (arterial line, CVC); daily sedation holds; spontaneous breathing trials when improving; early tracheostomy considered for prolonged ventilation; multidisciplinary input — respiratory, ICU, physiotherapy, nutrition team
severity_levels.mortality: 30-day mortality 20-30% for COPD requiring invasive ventilation; poor prognosis markers: pH <7.20, FEV1 <30% pre-morbid, multiple comorbidities, poor nutritional status

causative_agents_overview.viruses: 90-95% of acute bronchitis — rhinovirus, influenza, RSV, parainfluenza, coronavirus, metapneumovirus, adenovirus
causative_agents_overview.atypical_bacteria: 5-10% of acute bronchitis — Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis (important not to miss)
causative_agents_overview.typical_bacteria: Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis — important in AECB but rarely cause acute bronchitis in healthy people
causative_agents_overview.tobacco_smoke: Single most important cause of chronic bronchitis globally; causes cumulative irreversible airway injury
causative_agents_overview.indoor_air_pollution: Biomass fuel combustion (wood, dung, crop residue) — major cause of chronic bronchitis and COPD in India and developing countries; affects 3 billion people globally
causative_agents_overview.outdoor_air_pollution: PM2.5, ozone, nitrogen dioxide; significant contributor in Indian cities with extremely high pollution levels

pathophysiology.acute: Viral or bacterial infection of bronchial epithelium → inflammatory response (neutrophil and lymphocyte infiltration) → mucosal oedema → goblet cell hypersecretion of mucus → impaired mucociliary clearance → bronchial luminal narrowing and increased airway resistance → cough reflex activation (bronchial irritant receptors — C-fibres and A-delta fibres) → productive cough → recovery as immune response clears infection and epithelium regenerates (2-4 weeks)
pathophysiology.chronic: Repeated or chronic bronchial irritation (smoke, pollution) → sustained neutrophil and macrophage inflammation → protease/antiprotease imbalance → mucous gland hypertrophy and goblet cell hyperplasia (increased Reid index) → chronic mucus hypersecretion → ciliary dysfunction → repeated infections colonising abnormal airways → progressive airway wall remodelling (fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy) → irreversible airflow obstruction → air trapping → hyperinflation → increased work of breathing → impaired gas exchange → hypoxia → hypercapnia (advanced) → pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale (right heart failure)
pathophysiology.airway_remodelling: Chronic bronchitis is characterised by structural changes that are largely irreversible: subepithelial fibrosis (thickened basement membrane), smooth muscle hypertrophy, mucous gland enlargement, cartilage loss, and loss of alveolar wall attachments (emphysema component) that normally tether airways open during expiration

risk_factors: Cigarette smoking — single most important preventable risk factor for chronic bronchitis; 15-20 pack-years (1 pack per day × 20 years) typically needed for COPD development; risk proportional to total smoke exposure
Bidi smoking — Indian hand-rolled cigarettes; unfiltered and higher tobacco concentration per cigarette; extremely common in India; produces more tar and CO per cigarette than manufactured cigarettes

Biomass fuel indoor cooking (chulha) — wood, cow dung, coal, crop residue burning in poorly ventilated kitchens; affects millions of Indian rural women; equivalent smoke exposure to smoking >40 cigarettes per day; leading cause of COPD in non-smoking Indian women

Outdoor air pollution — PM2.5 levels in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Lucknow, Kanpur frequently exceed WHO guidelines by 10-20 times; chronic PM2.5 exposure causes bronchitis and accelerates COPD progression
Occupational exposures — coal miners, quarry workers, construction workers (silica), cotton textile workers (byssinosis), farmers, welders, chemical workers, wood workers
Viral respiratory infections — rhinovirus, influenza in winter; RSV in children; recurrent infections in childhood permanently impair lung development
Cold and damp environments — increases viral respiratory infection incidence; cold air is a direct airway irritant causing bronchospasm
Immunosuppression — HIV/AIDS, post-transplant, chemotherapy, high-dose corticosteroids — increased risk of severe and recurrent bronchitis
Pre-existing asthma — airway hyperresponsiveness increases susceptibility to viral bronchitis and risk of progression to COPD
Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency — genetic predisposition to early-onset emphysema and COPD; affects 1 in 2,000-5,000 Caucasians; screen in COPD presenting before age 45 or non-smokers
Poverty and low socioeconomic status — overcrowded housing (viral transmission), indoor cooking smoke, inability to afford clean fuels, access to healthcare
Low birth weight and preterm birth — impaired lung development in utero; reduced peak lung function; higher lifetime risk of COPD
Recurrent childhood respiratory infections — measles, RSV bronchiolitis, pertussis — can cause permanent airway remodelling and increased adult COPD risk
Passive smoking — involuntary inhalation of second-hand smoke; significantly increases bronchitis risk in children and non-smoking adults
Acid reflux (GORD/GERD) — gastro-oesophageal reflux causes aspiration of acid into airways (microaspiration) contributing to chronic cough and bronchitis

symptoms.overview: The cardinal symptom of bronchitis in all its forms is COUGH — the body's reflex to clear the inflamed, mucus-filled bronchial tubes. The character, duration, productivity, and associated features of the cough are the most important diagnostic clues. Acute bronchitis begins with an upper respiratory tract infection (runny nose, sore throat) followed by onset of cough in the first few days. Chronic bronchitis produces a 'morning cough' — the classical 'smoker's cough' — with gradual worsening dyspnoea over years. Understanding that cough in acute viral bronchitis normally lasts 2-3 weeks (and can persist to 4 weeks) prevents unnecessary anxiety, re-consultation, and antibiotic prescribing.

primary_symptoms.name: Cough — Productive (Wet) or Non-Productive (Dry)
primary_symptoms.description: The defining symptom of bronchitis. In acute bronchitis: begins as a dry, non-productive cough (first 2-3 days) then typically becomes productive with mucoid (white/clear) or mucopurulent (yellow-green) sputum. The shift to purulent sputum does NOT indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics — it reflects normal inflammatory response (neutrophil peroxidases). In chronic bronchitis: productive cough present most days (classically worst in the morning — pooled overnight secretions); characterised by large volumes of mucus coughed up on waking ('morning cough' — 'my engine needs clearing in the morning'). Cough reflex hypersensitivity (lowered cough threshold) persists for weeks post-infection explaining protracted cough.
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute: days 3-5 of URTI; Chronic: insidious over years
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Cough lasting >3 weeks in a non-smoker must be investigated to exclude: pertussis, atypical bacterial infection, post-nasal drip, GORD, eosinophilic bronchitis, asthma, lung cancer. Cough with haemoptysis (blood) ALWAYS requires investigation regardless of duration.

primary_symptoms.name: Sputum Production (Expectoration)
primary_symptoms.description: Mucus expelled from the lower respiratory tract by coughing. Character provides diagnostic clues: Clear/white mucoid sputum: viral bronchitis; early chronic bronchitis; asthma. Yellow/green mucopurulent sputum: increased neutrophil content from inflammation — common in both viral and bacterial bronchitis; does NOT automatically indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics. Rust-coloured (bloody) sputum: pneumococcal pneumonia; pulmonary embolism; requires chest X-ray urgently. Frank haematoptysis (blood): bronchiectasis; lung cancer; TB; pulmonary embolism — always requires investigation. Profuse clear watery sputum (bronchorrhoea): bronchoalveolar carcinoma (rare). Thick tenacious plugs: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA). Foul-smelling sputum: lung abscess; bronchiectasis with infected sputum.
primary_symptoms.note: Sputum colour alone should NOT determine antibiotic prescribing; clinical context, duration, severity, and patient factors are all essential

primary_symptoms.name: Wheeze (Bronchospasm)
primary_symptoms.description: A high-pitched musical expiratory sound produced by airflow through narrowed bronchi — caused by bronchial mucosal oedema, mucus plugging, and smooth muscle spasm in bronchitis. Wheeze is present in up to 40% of patients with acute bronchitis (often without underlying asthma). In acute viral bronchitis, temporary airway hyperresponsiveness and bronchospasm cause wheeze that resolves completely as the infection clears. In chronic bronchitis and COPD: wheeze reflects fixed and reversible airway obstruction. Important distinction: wheeze that does NOT resolve after an acute infection should prompt spirometry to investigate for asthma or COPD.
primary_symptoms.note: Unilateral wheeze (one-sided) suggests foreign body, tumour, or lymph node compression — always investigate

primary_symptoms.name: Dyspnoea (Breathlessness)
primary_symptoms.description: Breathlessness varies dramatically by bronchitis type and severity. In acute viral bronchitis: breathlessness on exertion is common; breathlessness at rest is unusual and requires investigation to exclude pneumonia. In chronic bronchitis: breathlessness is typically absent until GOLD II-III stage — patients subconsciously reduce activity to avoid breathlessness (the 'inactivity trap'); when present, the MRC dyspnoea scale (1-5) and mMRC scale quantify severity. GOLD IV chronic bronchitis: breathlessness at minimal exertion or rest; patient may be oxygen-dependent. In AECB: acute worsening of baseline dyspnoea is one of the three Anthonisen cardinal criteria.
mrc_dyspnoea_scale: Grade 1: Breathless with strenuous exercise only
Grade 2: Short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill
Grade 3: Walks slower than contemporaries on level ground due to breathlessness; has to stop to breathe when walking at own pace on level
Grade 4: Stops for breath after walking 100 metres or after a few minutes on level ground
Grade 5: Too breathless to leave the house; breathless when dressing and undressing
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute: gradual over days; Chronic: insidious over years

primary_symptoms.name: Fever and Systemic Symptoms
primary_symptoms.description: In acute bronchitis: LOW-GRADE fever (37.5-38.5°C) is common with viral infection; high fever (>39°C) is unusual and should prompt consideration of pneumonia or influenza. Accompanying URTI symptoms (runny nose, sore throat, sneezing) in the first 1-2 days distinguish viral bronchitis from atypical bacterial infection (Mycoplasma — more gradual onset, headache, and persistent dry cough). Myalgia (muscle aches), headache, and fatigue are systemic viral response symptoms. In chronic bronchitis: afebrile between exacerbations; fever with increased cough and sputum = AECB.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Moderate (acute); absent or mild (chronic)
primary_symptoms.note: High fever >39°C with cough and breathlessness — chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia is mandatory

primary_symptoms.name: Chest Tightness and Discomfort
primary_symptoms.description: Substernal or diffuse chest tightness from bronchial muscle spasm and inflammation — very common in acute bronchitis. Pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with breathing and coughing) is more typical of pneumonia or pleuritis than uncomplicated bronchitis. Severe chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw = cardiac origin — must always be excluded. Muscular intercostal pain from violent coughing bouts is a very common and benign cause of chest discomfort in bronchitis patients.
primary_symptoms.note: Central chest tightness with bronchospasm is a hallmark of viral bronchitis; pleuritic pain requires chest X-ray

secondary_symptoms: Runny nose and nasal congestion (rhinorrhoea) — preceding URTI phase; post-nasal drip can perpetuate cough
Sore throat (pharyngitis) — common in first 2-3 days of viral URTI preceding bronchitis
Headache — systemic viral response; CO2 retention headache (early morning, worse on waking) in advanced COPD with hypercapnia
Fatigue and malaise — universal in acute viral bronchitis; persistent in chronic bronchitis from hypoxia and systemic inflammation
Loss of appetite (anorexia) — systemic illness response; nutritional depletion is a major issue in advanced COPD (cachexia)
Ankle oedema — bilateral pitting oedema from cor pulmonale (right heart failure from pulmonary hypertension) in advanced chronic bronchitis/COPD
Cyanosis — blue discolouration of lips and fingernails from hypoxia; central cyanosis (lips, tongue) = serious hypoxaemia requiring oxygen
Barrel chest — increased AP diameter from lung hyperinflation in chronic emphysema; poor respiratory excursion
Pursed-lip breathing — spontaneous technique to generate intrinsic PEEP, preventing dynamic airway collapse during expiration in COPD
Use of accessory muscles of respiration — sternocleidomastoid, scalene, intercostal muscles visible during inspiration in moderate-severe AECB
Morning hoarseness — from overnight laryngeal oedema and mucus; common in post-nasal drip and GORD-related bronchitis
Night sweats and cough — consider tuberculosis (TB) in India — fever, night sweats, weight loss, haemoptysis, prolonged cough >2 weeks is TB until proven otherwise
Haemoptysis (coughing blood) — always requires investigation: bronchitis causes can include irritation from severe coughing bouts but lung cancer, TB, and pulmonary embolism must be excluded
warning_signs: Cough producing blood (haemoptysis) — regardless of quantity — must be investigated urgently with chest X-ray and possible bronchoscopy; exclude lung cancer, TB, pulmonary embolism
Dyspnoea at rest or in COPD patient worsening beyond usual baseline — possible AECB or pneumonia — same-day medical review
Oxygen saturation <92% on pulse oximeter — emergency oxygen and hospital review
Respiratory rate >25 breaths per minute — sign of significant respiratory distress
Confusion or altered consciousness in a COPD patient — possible CO2 retention (type 2 respiratory failure, CO2 narcosis) — EMERGENCY
Cough lasting more than 3-4 weeks — investigate: pertussis, TB (India), atypical bacteria, lung cancer, COPD, asthma, GORD, post-nasal drip
High fever >39°C with cough and breathlessness — possible pneumonia — chest X-ray required
New wheeze in a non-asthmatic over 40 years with smoking history — possible COPD — spirometry required
Ankle swelling with breathlessness in COPD patient — possible cor pulmonale or heart failure exacerbation
Unexplained weight loss with cough — possible lung cancer or TB — urgent investigation
whooping_cough_warning_signs: Paroxysmal coughing bouts (sudden uncontrollable severe coughing spells) — particularly diagnostic of pertussis
Post-tussive vomiting — vomiting after coughing fits (occurs in 50% of pertussis cases)
Inspiratory 'whoop' sound — classic whooping sound at end of cough paroxysm (more obvious in children than adults)
Cough persisting >2-3 weeks without improvement despite standard treatment

medical_history: Duration and onset of cough — days (acute viral); weeks (pertussis, atypical bacteria); months-years (chronic bronchitis); sudden worsening of pre-existing cough (AECB)
Character of cough — productive or dry; cough paroxysms (pertussis); nocturnal cough (asthma, GORD, post-nasal drip); morning cough on waking (chronic bronchitis)
Sputum character — colour (clear, white, yellow, green, blood-tinged); consistency; volume; change from baseline (AECB)
Haemoptysis — any blood in sputum, however small; red flag requiring urgent investigation (cancer, TB, PE)
Associated symptoms — fever, rhinorrhoea, sore throat (URTI preceding), wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness, hoarseness
Pertussis features — post-tussive vomiting, inspiratory whoop, coughing bouts, contact with whooping cough, vaccination history
Smoking history — current smoker? How many cigarettes/bidis per day? Total pack-year history (packs per day × years; one pack = 20 cigarettes). Previous quit attempts and methods.
Biomass fuel exposure — type of cooking fuel (wood, dung, LPG, electric); kitchen ventilation; hours per day cooking; how many years; relevant in Indian rural women especially
Occupational history — current and past occupations involving dust, chemical or fume exposure; pattern of symptoms relative to work (better on weekends/holidays = occupational)
Indoor air quality — gas cooking without extraction; damp housing; mould; pets
Previous bronchitis, pneumonia, or hospitalisation for respiratory illness — frequency and pattern; hospitalisations for respiratory illness in past 12 months (AECB frequency predicts future risk)
Known COPD or asthma — current medications; inhaler technique; compliance; peak flow; recent spirometry
Allergen history — seasonal variation (worsening in pollen season = allergic component); known allergens
Gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms — heartburn, acid regurgitation; nocturnal cough after eating (GORD-related cough)

Tuberculosis risk factors — close contact with TB; previous TB; HIV positive; recent travel to high-prevalence country; unexplained weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis (TB must be excluded in India — world's highest TB burden)

Medication history — ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril, ramipril) cause a persistent dry cough in up to 10-15% of patients — common cause of misdiagnosed 'bronchitis'; beta-blockers worsen bronchospasm in COPD/asthma
Travel history — TB exposure, fungal respiratory infections in endemic areas
Immunosuppression — HIV, transplant, chemotherapy, biologics; increases risk of severe opportunistic respiratory infections
Vaccination history — influenza (annual); pneumococcal (PPSV23 or PCV); pertussis (Tdap — have adult boosters been given?)
physical_examination: Vital signs — temperature (fever = AECB, pneumonia); respiratory rate (normal <20; tachypnoea >25 = significant distress); heart rate (tachycardia); blood pressure; oxygen saturation (SpO2 — must be measured with pulse oximeter in all respiratory assessments)

General appearance — distress level; use of accessory muscles of respiration (sternocleidomastoid, scalene visible during quiet breathing = severe); pursed-lip breathing (COPD); barrel chest (hyperinflation); cachexia (advanced COPD); cyanosis (peripheral at fingertips, central at lips and tongue — severe hypoxia)

INSPECTION: chest shape (barrel chest = hyperinflation); chest wall movement symmetry; intercostal indrawing (recession) during inspiration; paradoxical breathing (abdomen moves in during inspiration = severe diaphragmatic fatigue); respiratory rate and pattern

PALPATION: tracheal position (midline or deviated — pneumothorax, effusion); vocal fremitus (increased = consolidation/pneumonia; decreased = effusion, pleural thickening); chest expansion (reduced bilaterally in COPD)
PERCUSSION: hyperresonance (lung hyperinflation in COPD/emphysema — 'empty box' sound); dullness (consolidation or pleural effusion — suggests pneumonia complicating bronchitis)

AUSCULTATION (lung sounds): Wheeze (rhonchi) — high-pitched expiratory musical sounds from bronchospasm and narrowed airways (heard in bronchitis, COPD, asthma); Coarse crackles (crepitations) — early-to-mid inspiratory crackles from secretions and opening of small airways (bronchitis, bronchiectasis); Fine late inspiratory crackles — suggest pneumonia or fibrosis; Reduced or absent breath sounds — hyperinflated COPD or pleural effusion; Bronchial breathing — consolidation (pneumonia); Normal breath sounds — mild viral bronchitis may have entirely normal chest exam

Cardiovascular examination — elevated JVP (cor pulmonale); loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension); right ventricular heave; peripheral oedema (bilateral = cor pulmonale or CCF); hepatomegaly (right heart failure)
Clubbing of fingers — NOT a feature of simple bronchitis; its presence with cough suggests lung cancer, bronchiectasis, fibrosing alveolitis, or cyanotic congenital heart disease — always investigate
Upper respiratory tract — inspect oropharynx (erythema, exudate); nasal mucosa (congestion, polyps); postnasal drip (mucus on posterior pharyngeal wall); ears (bullous myringitis = Mycoplasma)
Lymph nodes — cervical lymphadenopathy (viral URTI, TB, lymphoma)
Body weight and BMI — weight loss in advanced COPD (cachexia worsens prognosis); BMI <20 in COPD = worse prognosis

diagnostic_tests.description: Non-invasive, immediate measurement of peripheral oxygen saturation — the percentage of haemoglobin that is oxygenated. Should be performed in ALL patients presenting with respiratory symptoms. A single most important triage tool for respiratory illness — identifies patients requiring oxygen therapy, hospital admission, or emergency intervention.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Immediate triage of hypoxia; guide oxygen therapy (target SpO2 94-98% in most; 88-92% in chronic hypercapnic COPD); identify need for hospital referral
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: SpO2 ≥96%: normal; SpO2 92-95%: mild hypoxia — monitor; SpO2 <92%: significant hypoxia — hospital review and supplemental oxygen; SpO2 <88%: severe hypoxia — emergency; TARGET in COPD on oxygen: 88-92% (avoid hyperoxia causing CO2 retention and Haldane effect)
diagnostic_tests.limitations: Unreliable in: poor peripheral perfusion (cold hands, shock); nail polish; dark skin (potential overestimation); carbon monoxide poisoning (CO-oxyhaemoglobin reads as oxyhaemoglobin — SpO2 falsely normal)

diagnostic_tests.description: The definitive investigation for confirming and quantifying chronic obstructive airway disease (chronic bronchitis/COPD). Patient takes maximum breath in and blows as hard and fast as possible into a spirometer measuring: FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second — airflow in first second); FVC (Forced Vital Capacity — total air expelled from full to empty lungs); FEV1/FVC ratio (Tiffeneau index — <0.70 post-bronchodilator confirms obstructive pattern = COPD); FEV1% predicted (determines COPD severity — GOLD I-IV). Spirometry is NOT required in uncomplicated acute bronchitis but IS the mandatory investigation for any suspected COPD or unexplained chronic cough.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose and stage COPD (chronic bronchitis); distinguish obstructive (COPD, asthma) from restrictive (fibrosis) lung disease; monitor progression; assess reversibility (bronchodilator response — significant if FEV1 improves >12% and >200mL post-bronchodilator suggesting asthma component)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: FEV1/FVC <0.70 post-bronchodilator = obstructive defect (COPD); FEV1 ≥80% predicted = GOLD I; 50-79% = GOLD II; 30-49% = GOLD III; <30% = GOLD IV; FEV1/FVC <0.70 with significant reversibility (>12% and 200mL improvement) = asthma more likely
diagnostic_tests.when_to_perform: Any adult with chronic cough (>8 weeks) and/or breathlessness; smoker over 40 with any respiratory symptoms; occupational exposure history; suspected COPD — spirometry is mandatory for COPD diagnosis (clinical diagnosis alone is insufficient)

diagnostic_tests.description: Chest X-ray is NOT required for diagnosis of straightforward acute bronchitis in otherwise healthy young adults. However, it is the most important investigation to EXCLUDE PNEUMONIA — which is clinically often indistinguishable from acute bronchitis and requires antibiotic treatment. Pneumonia presents with consolidation (opacity/shadowing) on CXR; bronchitis produces no specific abnormality on CXR (may show mildly increased bronchial markings or be entirely normal). CXR in chronic bronchitis/COPD shows: hyperinflation (flat diaphragm, increased AP diameter, widened rib spaces, reduced peripheral vascular markings); bullae (thin-walled emphysematous spaces); enlarged pulmonary arteries (pulmonary hypertension — cor pulmonale).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude pneumonia in patients with high fever, focal chest signs, or failure to improve; diagnose complications (pneumothorax, pleural effusion); baseline in chronic bronchitis; detect lung cancer (important differential for chronic cough in smokers)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal CXR: supports bronchitis diagnosis; Consolidation (lobar opacity/air bronchogram): pneumonia — requires antibiotics; Hyperinflation (flat diaphragm, increased intercostal spaces): COPD/emphysema; Hilar or lung mass: investigate for cancer; Cavity: TB, lung abscess
indications_in_acute_bronchitis: Focal chest signs (dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing)
Failure to improve with standard management after 7-10 days
Age >65 years with bronchitis (higher pneumonia risk)
Smoker >40 years (exclude lung cancer as cause of chronic cough)

diagnostic_tests.description: High-resolution CT of the chest provides detailed parenchymal and airway imaging beyond what chest X-ray can detect. In chronic bronchitis and COPD: HRCT shows: central and peripheral airway wall thickening; mucus plugging; emphysema (low-attenuation areas without visible walls); bronchiectasis (bronchial wall thickening and dilation). Used for complicated investigations — not routine in uncomplicated bronchitis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Characterise COPD pattern (emphysema-predominant vs airway-predominant); detect bronchiectasis; assess for lung cancer (low-dose CT screening for smokers in selected risk groups); detect ABPA; investigate recurrent haemoptysis
diagnostic_tests.indication: Recurrent bronchitis or suspected bronchiectasis; atypical COPD; haemoptysis with normal CXR; occupational lung disease assessment; pre-surgical COPD assessment

diagnostic_tests.description: Microbiological examination of expectorated sputum. In acute bronchitis: routine sputum culture is NOT recommended as it rarely changes management (viral aetiology undetectable; commensal bacteria confound interpretation). In AECB: sputum culture is valuable when: purulent sputum with no improvement after first-line antibiotics; GOLD III-IV severe COPD; recent hospitalisation (risk of MDR organisms); suspected Pseudomonas aeruginosa (very low FEV1, recent hospitalisation, structural lung disease); immunocompromised patients.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Guide antibiotic choice in AECB when first-line antibiotics fail; detect Pseudomonas and resistant organisms; TB detection (sputum AFB smear and culture — 3 early morning samples — for suspected pulmonary TB)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Significant: pure or predominant growth of a respiratory pathogen; Haemophilus influenzae (most common AECB pathogen); Streptococcus pneumoniae; Moraxella catarrhalis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa (severe COPD — requires anti-pseudomonal antibiotic); TB: acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on Ziehl-Neelsen stain and Mycobacterial culture
diagnostic_tests.tb_note: In India — ALWAYS consider TB in any cough lasting >2 weeks with fever, night sweats, or weight loss; 3 early morning sputum samples for AFB smear and Mycobacterial culture; GeneXpert (CBNAAT) available in India for rapid TB diagnosis and rifampicin resistance detection

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Nasopharyngeal Swab / Throat Swab — Viral and Pertussis PCR
diagnostic_tests.description: Nasopharyngeal or throat swab for PCR (polymerase chain reaction) testing. Multiplex respiratory virus PCR panels can simultaneously detect and identify: influenza A and B, RSV, rhinovirus, coronavirus (including SARS-CoV-2), parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, adenovirus within 2-4 hours. Bordetella pertussis PCR (nasopharyngeal swab) is the most sensitive test for whooping cough — best performed in the first 2-3 weeks of illness.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify specific virus in hospitalised patients (influenza — consider oseltamivir; RSV — consider palivizumab in high-risk infants); diagnose Bordetella pertussis; COVID-19 testing; infection control decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive influenza PCR: consider oseltamivir within 48 hours; Positive pertussis PCR: start azithromycin and notify public health
diagnostic_tests.indication: Hospitalised patients with bronchitis/lower respiratory infection; suspected pertussis (prolonged cough with paroxysms); COVID-19 testing; immunocompromised patients; COPD patients hospitalised with AECB (guides infection control and antiviral therapy)

diagnostic_tests.description: Serological testing for atypical respiratory bacteria — important when acute bronchitis is prolonged, severe, or unusual. IgM antibodies (acute infection) and IgG (past infection or rising titre in convalescent sample) measured for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose atypical bacterial bronchitis/pneumonia when standard investigations negative; guide macrolide or tetracycline antibiotic therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Mycoplasma IgM positive: acute Mycoplasma infection — treat with azithromycin; 4-fold rise in IgG titre between acute and convalescent samples (2-3 weeks apart) confirms recent infection
diagnostic_tests.note: Mycoplasma urine antigen test also available for Legionella (urinary Legionella antigen — serogroup 1 only)

diagnostic_tests.description: Blood count and inflammatory markers are useful primarily to distinguish bacterial from viral aetiology and to guide antibiotic prescribing decisions — particularly in AECB. Leucocytosis with neutrophilia suggests bacterial infection; normal WBC more consistent with viral. Lymphocytosis is characteristic of pertussis (peripheral lymphocytosis >10,000/mcL with characteristic lymphocyte morphology — 'lymphocytosis + prolonged cough = think pertussis'). CRP: low (<20 mg/L) suggests viral; elevated (>50 mg/L) suggests bacterial or significant inflammatory process.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Distinguish viral from bacterial aetiology; detect pertussis lymphocytosis; assess severity of infection; guide antibiotic decisions in AECB; eosinophilia (allergic/eosinophilic bronchitis)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC >12,000/mcL with neutrophilia: bacterial infection more likely; Lymphocytes >10,000/mcL: consider pertussis; Eosinophils >500/mcL: allergic component or eosinophilic bronchitis; CRP >50-100 mg/L: significant infection; CRP <20: likely viral — avoid antibiotics; Procalcitonin <0.1 ng/mL: viral — antibiotics unlikely beneficial

diagnostic_tests.description: Arterial blood sampling from the radial artery measuring: PaO2 (partial pressure of oxygen), PaCO2 (partial pressure of CO2), pH, HCO3- (bicarbonate), and oxygen saturation. Essential in moderate-severe AECB — identifies type of respiratory failure and guides oxygen therapy and NIV decisions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify type 1 (hypoxic — PaO2 <8 kPa, normal/low PaCO2) vs type 2 (hypercapnic — PaO2 <8 kPa + PaCO2 >6 kPa) respiratory failure; guide oxygen therapy target (SpO2 88-92% in known CO2 retainers); guide NIV initiation (pH <7.35 with hypercapnia); monitor response to treatment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Type 1 respiratory failure: PaO2 <8 kPa, normal or low PaCO2 — give oxygen to correct hypoxia; Type 2 respiratory failure: PaO2 <8 kPa + PaCO2 >6 kPa (hypercapnia) — controlled oxygen; NIV if pH <7.35; pH <7.25 on NIV = escalate to ICU/intubation
diagnostic_tests.indication: All hospitalised AECB; SpO2 <92%; confusion or drowsiness in COPD; any severe respiratory distress

diagnostic_tests.description: Procalcitonin is a peptide produced by bacterial infection (but not viral) — highly specific for bacterial infection. PCT-guided antibiotic therapy for ACUTE BRONCHITIS has been shown in multiple RCTs to safely reduce antibiotic use by 30-50% without worsening outcomes: PCT <0.1 ng/mL = viral — antibiotics strongly discouraged; PCT 0.1-0.25 = viral likely — antibiotics not recommended; PCT 0.25-0.5 = possible bacterial — consider antibiotics; PCT >0.5 = bacterial infection — antibiotics recommended.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Reduce inappropriate antibiotic use in acute bronchitis; distinguish viral from bacterial infection; guide antibiotic de-escalation in AECB; monitor treatment response
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: PCT <0.25 ng/mL: viral origin — antibiotics not indicated (acute bronchitis); PCT >0.5 ng/mL: bacterial infection likely — antibiotics indicated
diagnostic_tests.evidence: Cochrane review: PCT-guided therapy reduces antibiotic use in acute respiratory infections without increasing adverse outcomes; endorsed by WHO antibiotic stewardship programmes

diagnostic_tests.description: Simple portable device measuring the maximum speed of airflow during forced expiration. Primarily used in asthma to monitor airway obstruction and treatment response. In acute bronchitis with wheeze: PEFR may be reduced during the acute infection and should return to normal after recovery (persistent reduction after 4-6 weeks suggests underlying asthma or COPD — requires spirometry). PEFR compared to the patient's personal best determines severity of acute asthma.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for significant airflow obstruction; monitor acute bronchospasm; follow-up after acute bronchitis to identify underlying asthma or COPD
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: PEFR <80% predicted in acute bronchitis with wheeze: significant bronchospasm — consider bronchodilator; PEFR not recovering to predicted normal after 6 weeks: investigate with spirometry for COPD or asthma

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Mantoux Test / IGRA (Interferon-Gamma Release Assay) for Tuberculosis
diagnostic_tests.description: Tests for latent or active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Critically important in India — which has the world's highest TB burden. Any cough lasting more than 2 weeks with fever, night sweats, weight loss, or haemoptysis must be investigated for pulmonary TB before labelling as 'recurrent bronchitis'. Sputum AFB smear (×3 early morning specimens) and GeneXpert CBNAAT (combined TB diagnosis and rifampicin resistance detection) are now standard in India's Nikshay programme.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude pulmonary tuberculosis in prolonged cough; detect TB in high-risk contacts; GeneXpert provides rapid TB diagnosis and simultaneous rifampicin resistance testing
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: AFB smear positive: likely TB — treat; GeneXpert Xpert MTB/RIF positive: confirms TB and tests rifampicin resistance simultaneously; Negative AFB but clinical suspicion: TB culture (weeks), CT chest, bronchoscopy with BAL
diagnostic_tests.india_specific: TB remains endemic in India (2.5 million new cases per year); every case of prolonged cough (>2 weeks) in an Indian patient must be evaluated for TB before concluding bronchitis diagnosis; free TB diagnosis and treatment available under DOTS programme (Directly Observed Treatment Short-course) at all government health centres

diagnostic_tests.description: ECG is indicated in moderate-severe AECB to detect: cor pulmonale (right ventricular strain — right axis deviation, right bundle branch block, P pulmonale — tall peaked P waves in lead II, S1Q3T3 pattern); acute myocardial infarction (a precipitant of AECB or a COPD complication); atrial fibrillation (common in COPD exacerbation); and pulmonary embolism (tachycardia, right heart strain).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect cardiac complications of AECB; identify cor pulmonale; exclude cardiac cause of dyspnoea
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: P pulmonale (peaked P >2.5 mm in lead II) = right atrial enlargement in cor pulmonale; Right axis deviation + RBBB = right ventricular strain; S1Q3T3 pattern = pulmonary embolism

medicines.note: The most important principle in acute bronchitis management is antibiotic stewardship — over 90% of acute bronchitis is viral and does NOT benefit from antibiotics. Antibiotics cause side effects (GI upset, C. difficile colitis, allergic reactions), select resistant bacteria, and cost significant healthcare resources — all without shortening viral illness duration meaningfully. Treatment of acute bronchitis focuses on symptomatic relief: hydration, cough suppressants or expectorants, bronchodilators for wheeze, and antipyretics. For chronic bronchitis (COPD): regular inhaled bronchodilator therapy, smoking cessation, and pulmonary rehabilitation form the core. AECB: antibiotics + oral corticosteroids + bronchodilators for appropriate cases.
treatment_principles: 1. Acute bronchitis: DO NOT prescribe antibiotics in otherwise healthy adults — 90%+ is viral; antibiotics shorten cough by only 6-12 hours at the cost of significant side effects and resistance

2. EXCEPTIONS requiring antibiotics in acute bronchitis: confirmed pertussis (Bordetella pertussis) — azithromycin; confirmed Mycoplasma or Chlamydophila — macrolide or tetracycline; patient is immunocompromised, elderly, or has severe underlying lung disease with high fever and purulent sputum — consider antibiotics

3. AECB antibiotic indications: Anthonisen Type I (all 3 criteria: increased dyspnoea, sputum volume, purulence); Anthonisen Type II (2 of 3 criteria); any AECB requiring hospitalisation; severe COPD (GOLD III-IV) with any exacerbation
4. Oral corticosteroids in AECB: prednisolone 30-40mg daily for 5 days — shorten recovery time and reduce risk of treatment failure; use in all hospitalised AECB; consider in severe outpatient AECB

5. Bronchodilators: short-acting beta-2 agonists (salbutamol) are key rescue medication in all acute bronchitis with wheeze and in AECB; regular long-acting bronchodilators are the cornerstone of COPD maintenance
6. Smoking cessation is the most important treatment for chronic bronchitis — no medication matches the benefit; every consultation is an opportunity for cessation advice
7. Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): NOT indicated for acute bronchitis; indicated in COPD with frequent exacerbations (FEV1 <50% and >2 exacerbations per year); first-line in asthma
8. Controlled oxygen in COPD: target SpO2 88-92% (NOT 94-98%) in known COPD — hyperoxia causes CO2 retention (Haldane effect)

categories.purpose: Rapid relief of bronchospasm, wheeze, and dyspnoea in acute bronchitis with bronchoconstriction and in AECB.

medicines.name: Salbutamol (Albuterol) — Short-Acting Beta-2 Agonist (SABA)
medicines.form: MDI inhaler (100 mcg/actuation); nebuliser solution (2.5 mg/2.5 mL); dry powder inhaler; IV (severe acute asthma only)
medicines.dosage: MDI inhaler: 1-2 puffs (100-200 mcg) every 4-6 hours as needed; nebuliser: 2.5-5 mg in 2.5-5 mL normal saline every 4-6 hours (AECB/severe acute bronchospasm); maximum 4-6 hourly in stable disease; frequency can increase in acute exacerbation (continuous nebulisation in severe acute asthma)
medicines.use_case: Bronchospasm and wheeze in acute bronchitis; rescue bronchodilator in COPD (use as needed, not regular scheduled doses at GOLD I); AECB — foundation of nebulised bronchodilator treatment; acute asthma
medicines.mechanism: Beta-2 adrenoceptor agonist — selectively stimulates beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle causing relaxation and bronchodilation; onset 3-5 minutes; peak effect 30-60 minutes; duration 4-6 hours
medicines.inhaler_technique: Shake inhaler; breathe out fully; place in mouth or use spacer device; press canister while taking a slow deep breath; hold breath for 10 seconds; wait 30-60 seconds between puffs. SPACER (Aerochamber) markedly improves drug delivery and reduces oropharyngeal deposition — essential for children, elderly, and any patient with poor technique
side_effects: Hypokalaemia (important — monitor K+ in high-dose nebulised salbutamol with AECB)
medicines.note: High-dose salbutamol (>10 mg/hour via nebuliser) causes hypokalaemia — monitor electrolytes and replace potassium as needed

medicines.name: Ipratropium Bromide — Short-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist (SAMA)
medicines.form: MDI inhaler (20 mcg/actuation); nebuliser solution (0.5 mg/2 mL)
medicines.dosage: MDI: 2-4 puffs (40-80 mcg) every 6-8 hours; Nebuliser: 0.5 mg every 4-6 hours; often combined with salbutamol in AECB
medicines.use_case: AECB — synergistic bronchodilation when combined with salbutamol; COPD maintenance when LAMA not available; patients who cannot tolerate beta-2 agonists (severe cardiac disease); combined nebuliser (salbutamol + ipratropium) is standard AECB treatment in hospital
medicines.mechanism: Muscarinic receptor antagonist — blocks M3 muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle and submucosal glands; reduces bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion; longer onset than salbutamol but complementary mechanism
side_effects: Blurred vision if sprayed in eyes (do not use nebuliser mask — use mouthpiece)

categories.purpose: Long-acting bronchodilators are the foundation of COPD maintenance treatment — reduce breathlessness, improve exercise tolerance, reduce exacerbation frequency, and improve quality of life.

medicines.name: Tiotropium — Long-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist (LAMA)
medicines.form: Dry powder inhaler (18 mcg/capsule — HandiHaler device); Respimat inhaler (2.5 mcg/actuation — 2 puffs daily)
medicines.dosage: HandiHaler: one 18 mcg capsule inhaled once daily; Respimat: 2 × 2.5 mcg puffs once daily
medicines.use_case: First-line maintenance bronchodilator for COPD (GOLD II-IV) — recommended by GOLD guidelines as first COPD medication after short-acting rescue; dramatically reduces COPD exacerbation frequency (UPLIFT trial — 14% reduction in exacerbations); improves FEV1, 6-minute walk test, St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score
medicines.mechanism: Long-acting muscarinic receptor antagonist — blocks M3 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle with long duration (24 hours — once-daily dosing); dissociates slowly from M3 receptors
medicines.evidence: UPLIFT trial (Tashkin et al., NEJM 2008): tiotropium significantly reduced exacerbations, improved quality of life, and reduced respiratory hospitalisations compared to placebo over 4 years
side_effects: Urinary retention (elderly men with BPH — caution)
medicines.note: Do NOT swallow the capsule — pierce and inhale only; common error — always demonstrate inhaler technique; HandiHaler requires good manual dexterity — Respimat soft mist inhaler may be easier for elderly

medicines.name: Salmeterol — Long-Acting Beta-2 Agonist (LABA)
medicines.dosage: 50 mcg twice daily (via Accuhaler)
medicines.use_case: COPD maintenance — usually as LABA/ICS combination (salmeterol/fluticasone — Seretide) in GOLD III-IV with frequent exacerbations; LABA monotherapy increasingly replaced by LAMA in COPD; asthma maintenance (NEVER use as monotherapy without ICS in asthma — increased asthma death risk)
medicines.mechanism: Long-acting selective beta-2 agonist; prolonged bronchial smooth muscle relaxation for 12 hours
medicines.note: IMPORTANT: LABA should NOT be used as monotherapy in asthma — increased risk of asthma-related death (FDA black box warning); always combine with ICS in asthma; in COPD used as LABA alone or with ICS depending on eosinophil count

medicines.name: Formoterol / Eformoterol — LABA (twice daily or once daily)
medicines.dosage: 12 mcg twice daily
medicines.use_case: COPD and asthma maintenance; unique feature — faster onset than salmeterol (1-3 minutes vs 15-20 minutes) allowing use as rescue AND maintenance (MART — Maintenance And Reliever Therapy regimen in asthma using Symbicort)

medicines.name: Indacaterol — LABA (once daily)
medicines.form: Breezhaler DPI (150 mcg, 300 mcg once daily)
medicines.dosage: 150-300 mcg once daily
medicines.use_case: COPD maintenance — once-daily LABA; improves adherence; comparable to tiotropium and salmeterol for COPD; not used in asthma
medicines.side_effects: Cough after inhalation of capsule powder (characteristic — not harmful; resolves quickly)

medicines.name: Umeclidinium/Vilanterol (LAMA/LABA Combination — Anoro Ellipta)
medicines.form: Ellipta DPI (55 mcg umeclidinium + 22 mcg vilanterol once daily)
medicines.dosage: One inhalation once daily
medicines.use_case: GOLD C-D COPD — dual bronchodilation (LAMA + LABA) when single bronchodilator insufficient; evidence for LAMA + LABA combination superior to either agent alone for lung function and exacerbation reduction
medicines.note: GOLD 2023 guidelines recommend dual LAMA + LABA as initial therapy for many symptomatic COPD patients

categories.purpose: Reduce airway inflammation in COPD with frequent exacerbations (blood eosinophils ≥300/mcL) and in asthma (first-line); reduce exacerbation rate; NOT indicated for mild COPD or acute viral bronchitis.

medicines.name: Budesonide (ICS)
medicines.form: Turbuhaler DPI (100, 200, 400 mcg/dose); MDI; nebuliser (1 mg/2 mL — for AECB as alternative to oral prednisolone)
medicines.dosage: COPD: 200-400 mcg twice daily; Asthma (low dose): 200-400 mcg/day; moderate: 400-800 mcg/day; high: >800 mcg/day; Nebuliser (AECB): 1-2 mg twice daily as alternative to oral prednisolone
medicines.use_case: ICS component in COPD with blood eosinophils ≥100/mcL + ≥2 exacerbations per year; first-line asthma treatment; available as nebuliser for AECB when oral route not preferred
side_effects: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) — rinse mouth with water after use; use spacer device
Dysphonia (hoarse voice) — local deposition on vocal cords
Increased pneumonia risk in COPD (significant and well-documented — particularly fluticasone; lower risk with budesonide)
Systemic effects at very high doses: adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, skin thinning

medicines.name: Budesonide/Formoterol (ICS/LABA — Symbicort)
medicines.dosage: COPD: 400/12 mcg twice daily; Asthma maintenance: 200/6 mcg twice daily; SMART regimen (asthma only): 200/6 mcg as both maintenance and reliever (maximum 8 puffs per day)
medicines.use_case: GOLD C-D COPD with eosinophilia; moderate-severe asthma maintenance; SMART regimen (Symbicort Maintenance And Reliever Therapy) in asthma — single inhaler replaces ICS + SABA
medicines.evidence: SMART regimen reduces asthma exacerbations more effectively than fixed-dose ICS/LABA + separate rescue SABA

medicines.name: Fluticasone/Salmeterol (ICS/LABA — Seretide/Advair)
medicines.form: Accuhaler DPI (100/50, 250/50, 500/50 mcg per dose); MDI Evohaler
medicines.dosage: COPD: Accuhaler 500/50 mcg twice daily; Asthma: dose of ICS component depends on severity
medicines.use_case: COPD GOLD C-D; moderate-severe asthma; twice-daily dosing
medicines.note: Fluticasone propionate has higher pneumonia risk in COPD compared to budesonide — monitor for respiratory infections; consider de-escalation if no eosinophilia

medicines.name: Fluticasone Furoate/Vilanterol (ICS/LABA — once daily)
medicines.dosage: One inhalation once daily
medicines.use_case: Once-daily COPD and asthma management — improves adherence; Ellipta inhaler is simple to use

medicines.name: Beclomethasone (ICS)
medicines.dosage: Asthma: 200-400 mcg twice daily (low-medium dose); COPD: 200-400 mcg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Widely available and lower cost ICS; first-line ICS in asthma in many developing countries including India
medicines.note: CFC-free (HFA) formulations have smaller particle size — slightly different deposition from older CFC formulations — doses may not be directly interchangeable between brands; seek specialist advice when switching

categories.category_name: Antibiotics — For Acute Bacterial Bronchitis (Pertussis, Atypical Bacteria) and AECB
categories.purpose: Targeted antibiotic therapy for the minority of bronchitis cases requiring antibiotics: confirmed bacterial aetiology (pertussis, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila); AECB meeting antibiotic criteria; severe COPD exacerbation.
categories.notes: Pertussis and atypical bacteria (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila) require macrolides or tetracyclines — beta-lactams (amoxicillin, penicillin) are INEFFECTIVE. AECB antibiotics: cover H. influenzae (most common), S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis; amoxicillin or doxycycline are first-line.

medicines.name: Azithromycin
medicines.dosage: Pertussis: 500 mg day 1, then 250 mg days 2-5 (5-day course); Atypical bacteria (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila): 500 mg once daily for 5 days; AECB (mild-moderate): 500 mg once daily for 3-5 days; Prophylaxis in frequent AECB: 250 mg three times per week (long-term, with ECG monitoring — QT prolongation risk)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for pertussis (whooping cough); first-line for Mycoplasma and Chlamydophila pneumoniae bronchitis; alternative antibiotic in AECB (particularly penicillin-allergic patients or when atypical organisms suspected); long-term prophylaxis to reduce AECB frequency in GOLD III-IV COPD (>2 exacerbations/year)
medicines.mechanism: Macrolide antibiotic — inhibits 50S ribosomal subunit; bacteriostatic; tissue penetration into respiratory secretions is excellent (intracellular penetration important for atypical organisms); anti-inflammatory effects independent of antimicrobial activity
medicines.resistance_warning: Macrolide resistance in Mycoplasma pneumoniae is increasing (20-80% in some Asian countries) — doxycycline is an important alternative
medicines.prophylaxis_evidence: ALBERT trial (NEJM 2011): azithromycin 250mg daily for 1 year in COPD patients with frequent exacerbations reduced AECB rate by 27% and improved quality of life; ECG monitoring required (QTc interval — do not use if QTc >450 ms)
side_effects: QT prolongation (screen ECG before long-term use)

medicines.name: Doxycycline
medicines.dosage: Atypical bacteria: 100 mg twice daily for 7-14 days; AECB (first or second-line): 200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
medicines.use_case: Mycoplasma pneumoniae bronchitis (particularly where macrolide resistance suspected); Chlamydophila pneumoniae; first-line or alternative oral antibiotic in AECB (excellent activity against H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis, and atypicals in one agent); preferred for prolonged-release formulation available
medicines.mechanism: Tetracycline antibiotic — inhibits 30S ribosomal subunit; bacteriostatic; broad spectrum including atypical bacteria
contraindications: Pregnancy — affects fetal bone and tooth development (permanent tooth discolouration)
side_effects: Oesophageal ulceration — take with full glass of water and remain upright for 30 minutes

medicines.name: Amoxicillin
medicines.dosage: AECB: 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
medicines.use_case: First-line antibiotic for AECB with Anthonisen Type I-II criteria when atypical organisms NOT suspected and when penicillin-susceptible organisms expected; covers H. influenzae (most common AECB pathogen — 50-70% susceptible), S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis (30% produce beta-lactamase — resistant)
medicines.mechanism: Aminopenicillin — broad-spectrum beta-lactam; inhibits cell wall synthesis; bactericidal
medicines.resistance_note: H. influenzae beta-lactamase production is increasing; Moraxella catarrhalis is 90-95% beta-lactamase producing (resistant to amoxicillin alone); if treatment failure — switch to co-amoxiclav or doxycycline
medicines.note: NOT effective for pertussis, Mycoplasma, or Chlamydophila — use macrolide or tetracycline for these organisms

medicines.name: Co-Amoxiclav (Amoxicillin-Clavulanate)
medicines.dosage: 625 mg three times daily for 5-7 days (AECB)
medicines.use_case: AECB when beta-lactamase-producing organisms suspected (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, Staph aureus); penicillin failure in AECB; more reliable activity than amoxicillin alone against common AECB pathogens; also covers anaerobes
side_effects: Cholestatic jaundice (rare — caution if previous co-amoxiclav-related jaundice)

medicines.name: Clarithromycin
medicines.dosage: 250-500 mg twice daily for 5-7 days; Modified release: 500 mg once daily for 7 days
medicines.use_case: Atypical bacterial bronchitis (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila); AECB with penicillin allergy; Legionella pneumophila (atypical pneumonia); covers H. influenzae better than erythromycin
medicines.mechanism: Macrolide antibiotic; 50S ribosomal inhibition; long half-life; excellent intracellular penetration
side_effects: Nausea, metallic taste, GI upset (less than erythromycin)
Drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitor — increases levels of warfarin, statins, digoxin, carbamazepine)

medicines.name: Levofloxacin / Moxifloxacin (Respiratory Fluoroquinolones)
medicines.dosage: Levofloxacin: 500-750 mg once daily for 5-7 days; Moxifloxacin: 400 mg once daily for 5-7 days
medicines.use_case: AECB when: penicillin allergy; co-amoxiclav failure; more severe COPD exacerbation; Pseudomonas risk (levofloxacin preferred — better pseudomonal activity); 'respiratory quinolones' with excellent coverage of H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, atypicals, and Legionella in one agent
medicines.mechanism: Fluoroquinolone — inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; bactericidal; excellent respiratory tissue penetration
medicines.reserve_note: Fluoroquinolones should be reserved for severe exacerbations — routine use for mild AECB increases resistance; Moxifloxacin has NO activity against Pseudomonas — use levofloxacin if Pseudomonas suspected (severe COPD, prior Pseudomonas isolation, hospitalisation)

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin (for Pseudomonas-Risk AECB)
medicines.dosage: 500-750 mg twice daily for 7-10 days; IV 400 mg every 8-12 hours (hospitalised, severe)
medicines.use_case: AECB in severe COPD (FEV1 <30%) where Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a concern: previous Pseudomonas isolation; recent hospitalisation; structural lung disease (bronchiectasis); recent broad-spectrum antibiotic course; FEV1 <30% predicted
medicines.note: Ciprofloxacin covers Pseudomonas but has poor pneumococcal activity — only use when Pseudomonas is specifically a concern

categories.purpose: Accelerate recovery and reduce treatment failure in AECB — shorten duration of hospitalisation and hasten improvement in lung function.

medicines.name: Prednisolone (Oral)
medicines.dosage: 30-40 mg once daily for 5 days (AECB — GOLD and NICE recommended); NOT longer unless clinical necessity — no benefit of longer courses (REDUCE trial evidence); higher doses (60 mg) NOT shown superior to 30-40 mg; no tapering required for 5-day course
medicines.use_case: All hospitalised AECB; outpatient AECB in GOLD III-IV COPD or not responding to bronchodilators alone; accelerates FEV1 improvement and reduces treatment failure risk by 30%
medicines.mechanism: Glucocorticoid — inhibits NF-κB and AP-1 transcription factors; reduces cytokine production (IL-8, TNF-alpha, IL-1β) and neutrophil infiltration in airways; reduces mucosal oedema and airway hyperresponsiveness
medicines.evidence: REDUCE trial (Leuppi et al., JAMA 2013): 5-day prednisolone course non-inferior to 14-day course for AECB — shorter course recommended
side_effects: Hyperglycaemia (significant in diabetics — monitor blood glucose closely and adjust insulin/hypoglycaemic agents)
Short-term: minimal risk; prolonged courses: adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, weight gain, cataracts
medicines.note: In diabetics with AECB: prednisolone causes significant hyperglycaemia — monitor blood glucose four times daily; may need insulin sliding scale; do NOT withhold steroids if clinically indicated — manage glucose aggressively

medicines.name: Hydrocortisone (IV) — For Hospitalised Unable to Take Oral
