medicines.dosage: 200 mg IV every 6 hours OR 100 mg IV every 6-8 hours until oral route established; convert to oral prednisolone 40 mg as soon as tolerating
medicines.use_case: Severe AECB requiring ICU; unable to take oral medication; NIV with altered consciousness
medicines.note: Switch to oral prednisolone as soon as possible — IV hydrocortisone is equivalent but more inconvenient

categories.purpose: Reduce distressing, non-productive cough in acute bronchitis when cough is causing significant sleep disturbance, chest wall pain, or social disruption. Use selectively — productive cough with sputum should generally NOT be suppressed as expectoration clears infection.

medicines.name: Dextromethorphan (DXM)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 10-30 mg every 4-6 hours (max 120 mg/day); Children 6-12 years: 5-10 mg every 4-6 hours
medicines.use_case: Non-productive dry cough in acute viral bronchitis causing sleep disturbance; temporary cough suppression when productive cough has cleared
medicines.mechanism: NMDA receptor antagonist and sigma-1 receptor agonist in cough centre of brainstem; centrally-acting antitussive
side_effects: Risk of misuse/abuse in higher doses (dissociative effects)
medicines.note: NOT recommended in children under 6 years; has weak evidence for efficacy but widely used; honey is as effective in studies and safer

medicines.name: Pholcodine
medicines.dosage: Adults: 5-10 mg three to four times daily
medicines.use_case: Non-productive irritating dry cough; mild centrally-acting antitussive; less abuse potential than codeine
medicines.mechanism: Opioid receptor agonist in brainstem cough centre; peripherally restricted — does not cause analgesia at standard doses
medicines.note: Being progressively withdrawn from some markets due to potential IgE sensitisation and anaphylaxis risk with neuromuscular blocking agents; check current regulatory status in your region

medicines.name: Honey (Natural Antitussive — First-Line in Children)
medicines.form: Raw honey or mixed in warm water/tea
medicines.dosage: Children 1-5 years: ½ teaspoon at bedtime; Children 6-12 years: 1 teaspoon at bedtime; Adults: 1-2 teaspoons as needed
medicines.use_case: Acute cough in children and adults — evidence from multiple RCTs shows honey equals or exceeds dextromethorphan for reducing nocturnal cough severity and sleep disturbance; safe, natural, widely available, and inexpensive
medicines.mechanism: Demulcent (soothes irritated mucosa); antimicrobial properties (hydrogen peroxide, low pH, osmotic effect); antioxidant polyphenols; antibacterial effect (Manuka honey — methylglyoxal)
medicines.evidence: Paul et al. (Archives of Pediatrics 2007): buckwheat honey superior to dextromethorphan for nocturnal cough in children; Cochrane review: honey may be slightly more effective than no treatment, DXM, and placebo for acute cough
medicines.warning: NEVER give honey to infants under 12 months — risk of infant botulism (Clostridium botulinum spores in honey can proliferate in immature gut)

categories.purpose: Reduce sputum viscosity (mucolytics) or stimulate mucus production and expectoration (expectorants) to facilitate clearance of respiratory secretions.

medicines.name: Carbocisteine (Carbomethylcysteine)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 750 mg three times daily initially; reduce to 375 mg three times daily for maintenance; Children: 62.5-250 mg three to four times daily (weight-based)
medicines.use_case: Reducing sputum viscosity in chronic bronchitis and COPD — long-term use reduces AECB frequency; symptomatic relief in acute bronchitis with tenacious sputum; chronic bronchiectasis
medicines.mechanism: Mucolytic — reduces disulphide bonds in mucus glycoproteins; reduces sputum viscosity and elasticity; improves mucociliary transport; stimulates serous gland secretion to liquefy secretions
medicines.evidence: PEACE trial (Zheng JP et al., Lancet 2008): carbocisteine significantly reduced AECB frequency in Chinese COPD patients; anti-inflammatory effects may also contribute

medicines.name: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) — Oral
medicines.dosage: COPD mucolytic: 600 mg once daily; Acute bronchitis: 200 mg three times daily or 600 mg once daily; High-dose NAC: 600 mg twice daily (some evidence for COPD exacerbation reduction)
medicines.use_case: Mucolytic in acute and chronic bronchitis — reduces sputum viscosity; antioxidant (glutathione precursor) — reduces oxidative stress in COPD airways; long-term use may modestly reduce AECB frequency particularly in patients not using ICS (PANTHEON trial); IV high-dose NAC: antidote for paracetamol overdose
medicines.mechanism: Mucolytic — reduces disulphide bonds in mucus glycoproteins; antioxidant — donates sulfhydryl group to replenish intracellular glutathione; anti-inflammatory
medicines.evidence: Meta-analysis (Tse et al.): NAC reduces AECB frequency (RR 0.69); most benefit in patients with FEV1 >50% and those not on ICS
side_effects: Nausea (effervescent formulation dissolves unpleasant smell of sulphur — mix with juice)
Bronchospasm (rare — from inhaled NAC; oral generally well-tolerated)

medicines.name: Bromhexine
medicines.dosage: Adults: 8-16 mg three times daily; Children: 4-8 mg three times daily
medicines.use_case: Mucolytic for productive cough in acute bronchitis, chronic bronchitis, and COPD; metabolised to ambroxol (active metabolite) in the body; commonly used in India; safe and well-tolerated
medicines.mechanism: Stimulates serous gland secretion to liquefy mucus; may stimulate surfactant production; ambroxol metabolite stimulates mucociliary clearance

medicines.name: Ambroxol
medicines.dosage: Adults: 30 mg three times daily (first 3 days); then 30 mg twice daily for maintenance; Children: 7.5-15 mg three times daily
medicines.use_case: Active metabolite of bromhexine; mucolytic and mucokinetic (stimulates mucociliary transport); stimulates surfactant synthesis in alveolar type II cells; widely prescribed in India for acute bronchitis — one of the most commonly used respiratory medications
medicines.mechanism: Stimulates serous secretion; increases ciliary beat frequency; stimulates surfactant production; local anaesthetic effect (reduces cough trigger sensitivity)

medicines.name: Guaifenesin (Glyceryl Guaiacolate) — Expectorant
medicines.dosage: Adults: 200-400 mg every 4 hours (max 2.4 g/day); Children: 100-200 mg every 4 hours
medicines.use_case: Expectorant for productive cough in acute bronchitis — stimulates mucus secretion to make sputum less viscous; increases mucus transport up the airway (mucokinetic); most commonly used OTC respiratory ingredient in combination cough syrups
medicines.mechanism: Stimulates gastric mucosal irritant receptors → vagal reflex increases respiratory tract secretions → dilutes and loosens sputum; mucokinetic effect
medicines.note: Evidence for clinical efficacy is modest; ensure adequate hydration (additional 2L/day) to maximise expectorant effect

categories.purpose: Reduce severity and duration of influenza-induced bronchitis and lower respiratory illness when initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset.

medicines.name: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 75 mg twice daily for 5 days; Children (weight-based): <15 kg: 30 mg twice daily; 15-23 kg: 45 mg twice daily; 23-40 kg: 60 mg twice daily; >40 kg: 75 mg twice daily; Prophylaxis: 75 mg once daily for 10 days (post-exposure)
medicines.use_case: Influenza A and B — recommended for: hospitalised patients with influenza; high-risk groups (elderly >65, pregnant women, COPD, immunocompromised, BMI >40, diabetes, chronic heart or renal disease); severe influenza regardless of timing; ideally initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset for maximum benefit
medicines.mechanism: Neuraminidase inhibitor — blocks influenza neuraminidase enzyme preventing viral particle release from infected cells and spread to new cells; reduces viral shedding duration by ~50%
medicines.evidence: Reduces hospitalisation risk by 50% and ICU admission by 30% when given within 48 hours in high-risk patients; NICE recommends in all hospitalised influenza patients regardless of time since onset
side_effects: Rare: neuropsychiatric effects (delirium, self-harm impulses) — mostly children; monitor

medicines.name: Zanamivir (Relenza)
medicines.dosage: Adults and children ≥5 years: 2 inhalations (10 mg) twice daily for 5 days; prophylaxis: 2 inhalations once daily for 10 days
medicines.use_case: Influenza A and B treatment; alternative to oseltamivir when oral route not feasible; particularly useful in oseltamivir-resistant influenza (rare); NOT suitable for patients with reactive airways (bronchospasm risk)
medicines.contraindications: COPD and asthma (risk of severe bronchospasm — use oseltamivir instead)
medicines.mechanism: Inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor — delivers drug directly to respiratory tract

categories.purpose: The most important pharmacological intervention in chronic bronchitis — smoking cessation at any stage of COPD significantly slows disease progression and is the only intervention proven to reduce long-term mortality in COPD.
categories.evidence: LUNG HEALTH STUDY (NEJM 1994): Smoking cessation reduced FEV1 decline from ~60 mL/year to ~30 mL/year — effectively halving the rate of COPD progression; no pharmacological agent comes close to matching this benefit.

medicines.name: Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT)
medicines.form: Transdermal patch (7 mg, 14 mg, 21 mg/24 hours); chewing gum (2 mg, 4 mg); sublingual tablet; nasal spray; inhaler; lozenge
medicines.dosage: Patch: 21 mg/24 hours for 6 weeks (>20 cigarettes/day), then step down to 14 mg, then 7 mg; or 14 mg if <20 cigarettes/day; Gum: 2-4 mg as needed (max 24 pieces/day); duration 8-12 weeks total
medicines.use_case: Smoking cessation in all smokers with chronic bronchitis or COPD; combination NRT (patch + gum or lozenge) more effective than single form; available OTC; safe in most patients including most cardiac patients
medicines.mechanism: Provides nicotine to reduce withdrawal symptoms (irritability, anxiety, craving, difficulty concentrating) without tobacco toxins; allows behavioural habit change while managing physical nicotine dependence
medicines.evidence: NRT doubles quit rates compared to willpower alone; combination NRT (long-acting patch + short-acting gum) superior to single-form NRT
side_effects: Patch: skin irritation at application site; vivid dreams (remove patch at night if disturbed sleep)
Gum: jaw ache; hiccups; nausea (use correct 'chew and park' technique)

medicines.name: Varenicline (Champix / Chantix)
medicines.dosage: Week 1: 0.5 mg once daily (days 1-3), then 0.5 mg twice daily (days 4-7); Week 2 onwards: 1 mg twice daily; Total duration: 12 weeks (extend to 24 weeks for sustained abstinence); Set quit date for 1-2 weeks after starting
medicines.use_case: Most effective pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation — quit rates approximately triple compared to placebo; recommended by NICE as first-line pharmacotherapy; also effective for tobacco use in smokeless tobacco/bidi users; can be used in COPD
medicines.mechanism: Partial agonist at alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor — reduces craving and withdrawal symptoms (partial agonist effect) AND blocks pleasure from smoking (receptor occupancy blocks nicotine binding); dual mechanism makes it most effective cessation medication
medicines.evidence: Meta-analyses: varenicline approximately doubles quit rates at 1 year compared to NRT; EAGLES trial (Cahill et al.): safe in psychiatric populations — no significant increase in serious neuropsychiatric events vs placebo
side_effects: Nausea (most common — take with food; usually improves after 1-2 weeks)
Insomnia and abnormal dreams (take 1 mg at lunchtime rather than evening if severe)
Previously: concerns about suicidal ideation and cardiovascular events — subsequent large trials (EAGLES) showed no significant increase vs placebo; still requires counselling
medicines.contraindications: Caution in severe renal impairment (dose reduction); caution in history of seizures; discuss risks and benefits in psychiatric history

medicines.name: Bupropion Sustained-Release (Zyban)
medicines.dosage: 150 mg once daily for 6 days, then 150 mg twice daily for 7-12 weeks; Set quit date 10-14 days after starting
medicines.use_case: Second-line smoking cessation medication; effective in COPD smokers; also an antidepressant (NDRI) — may benefit smokers with comorbid depression
medicines.mechanism: Noradrenaline-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) and nicotinic receptor antagonist — reduces craving and withdrawal symptoms via dopaminergic reward pathway modulation; nicotinic antagonism reduces satisfaction from smoking
side_effects: Seizures — CONTRAINDICATED with seizure disorder, eating disorder, or MAOIs (seizure threshold lowered)

medicines.name: Roflumilast (PDE4 Inhibitor)
medicines.dosage: 500 mcg once daily
medicines.use_case: Add-on therapy in GOLD III-IV COPD with chronic bronchitis phenotype (productive cough) and ≥2 exacerbations per year despite LAMA + LABA + ICS triple therapy; reduces exacerbation frequency by approximately 15-20%; particularly effective in patients with blood eosinophils >150/mcL or FEV1 <50%
medicines.mechanism: Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor — increases intracellular cAMP in inflammatory cells (neutrophils, macrophages, T-lymphocytes) → reduces neutrophil migration and cytokine production → reduces airway inflammation; an anti-inflammatory drug, NOT a bronchodilator
medicines.evidence: TRILOGY and REACT trials: roflumilast added to combination inhaler therapy further reduced severe exacerbations in high-risk COPD patients
side_effects: Diarrhoea and nausea (very common — first few weeks; usually resolves)
Weight loss (average 2 kg — monitor in underweight COPD patients)
Contraindicated in: moderate-severe hepatic impairment; depression with suicidal ideation

medicines.name: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) Augmentation Therapy
medicines.dosage: 60 mg/kg IV weekly
medicines.use_case: COPD from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (ZZ or SZ genotype) with FEV1 25-80% predicted — IV AAT augmentation therapy reduces emphysema progression (CT volumetric imaging); expensive and not widely available in India
medicines.note: Must confirm AAT deficiency genotype before initiating; currently not available or reimbursed in India

medicines.name: Theophylline (Methylxanthine)
medicines.dosage: Adults: theophylline 400 mg modified-release once at night (start low); titrate according to serum theophylline levels (target 10-20 mg/L); dose varies by smoking status, age, liver disease, and drug interactions
medicines.use_case: Third-line bronchodilator in COPD when LAMA/LABA/ICS maximum therapy insufficient; acute severe asthma/AECB (IV aminophylline — hospital use); low-resource settings where modern inhalers unaffordable
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective PDE inhibitor and adenosine receptor antagonist — bronchodilation; respiratory muscle stimulation (improves diaphragm contractility — useful in severe COPD); mild anti-inflammatory effects; increases mucociliary clearance
medicines.monitoring: Serum theophylline levels — NARROW THERAPEUTIC WINDOW; toxic above 20 mg/L; many drug interactions (erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, allopurinol increase levels; rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, smoking decrease levels); check levels at 5-7 days and after any relevant drug change
side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, headache (common; early signs of toxicity)
Toxic levels (>20 mg/L): seizures, ventricular arrhythmias — life-threatening; monitor carefully
medicines.note: Largely superseded by modern inhaled therapy in high-income settings; still widely used in India and low-resource settings

categories.purpose: Augments breathing in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (type 2) complicating AECB — reduces work of breathing, improves gas exchange, and avoids invasive intubation with its complications.

medicines.name: BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) — Non-Invasive Ventilation
medicines.form: Non-invasive ventilator via tight-fitting face mask
medicines.dosage: Initial settings: IPAP (Inspiratory Positive Airway Pressure) 10-15 cmH2O; EPAP (Expiratory Positive Airway Pressure) 3-5 cmH2O; titrate to clinical response (target RR <25, pH >7.35, improved consciousness)
medicines.use_case: First-line treatment for hypercapnic respiratory failure in AECB when pH <7.35 and pCO2 >6 kPa; reduces need for intubation by 50%; reduces ICU mortality; evidence-based and highly recommended by GOLD and BTS guidelines; most effective when started early (pH 7.25-7.35 — better outcomes than pH <7.25)
medicines.mechanism: IPAP: provides pressure support during inspiration — reduces work of breathing and helps overcome auto-PEEP; EPAP: prevents alveolar collapse and improves FRC; overall reduces respiratory muscle fatigue and improves CO2 clearance
medicines.evidence: Brochard et al. NEJM 1995: NIV reduced intubation rate from 74% to 26% in AECOPD with respiratory failure; reduces in-hospital mortality by 50%; reduces 2-month mortality
contraindications_for_NIV: Respiratory arrest or arrest imminent (needs intubation)
Uncooperative patient who cannot tolerate mask
Vomiting with aspiration risk (use airway protection/intubation)
medicines.note: If NIV failing (pH <7.25 despite optimal NIV, worsening consciousness) — escalate to invasive mechanical ventilation or consider ceiling of treatment discussion

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Nutrition plays a critically important but often overlooked role in bronchitis management — particularly in chronic bronchitis and COPD. Acute viral bronchitis: nutritional support assists immune function and recovery. Chronic bronchitis/COPD: malnutrition (cachexia) is extremely common and independently predicts worse outcomes and higher mortality. Up to 40% of outpatients and 70% of hospitalised COPD patients have significant nutritional depletion. Additionally, dietary patterns influence airway inflammation, antioxidant defences, and respiratory muscle strength — key factors in both acute and chronic bronchitis.

nutritional_principles_by_form.acute_bronchitis: Focus on immune support, adequate hydration (thins mucus), and foods that soothe inflamed airways; avoid foods that thicken mucus or irritate airways
nutritional_principles_by_form.chronic_bronchitis_copd: Maintain healthy body weight (both underweight AND obesity are harmful); adequate protein intake (preserves respiratory muscle mass); anti-inflammatory Mediterranean-style diet; adequate micronutrients (Vitamin D, Vitamin C, antioxidants); appropriate carbohydrate-fat ratio (lower carbohydrate reduces CO2 production from metabolism — important in CO2 retainers); small frequent meals (large meals cause diaphragmatic elevation worsening dyspnoea)

recommended_foods.category: Hydration — The Most Immediate Dietary Intervention in Acute Bronchitis
recommended_foods.evidence: Adequate hydration reduces sputum viscosity, improves mucociliary transport, and facilitates expectoration — critical for recovery from acute bronchitis

items.food: Warm water with honey and lemon
items.benefit: Most evidence-based home remedy for bronchitis cough; honey: demulcent (soothes inflamed mucosa), antimicrobial (hydrogen peroxide, methylglyoxal), antioxidant; lemon: Vitamin C (immune support), acidifies sputum slightly improving expectoration; warmth: thins mucus, soothes bronchial irritation, induces mild bronchodilation
items.frequency: 3-5 times daily during acute illness; as needed for chronic cough

items.food: Ginger tea (Adrak chai — Indian style or plain ginger tea)
items.benefit: 6-gingerol and 6-shogaol — anti-inflammatory (COX-2 inhibition); bronchodilatory effect (relaxes airway smooth muscle in vitro); antiemetic (useful when cough triggers vomiting); mucolytic effect (loosens mucus); antiviral properties (inhibits rhinovirus and RSV attachment in vitro); 'adrak-tulsi chai' (ginger-holy basil tea) — traditional Indian remedy with convergent scientific rationale
items.frequency: 3-5 cups daily during acute bronchitis; 1-2 cups daily for chronic cough

items.benefit: Eugenol and ursolic acid — anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial; expectorant properties; adaptogenic (reduces stress-related immune suppression); bronchodilatory effects (in animal studies); Tulsi tea is a culturally significant traditional remedy in India with growing scientific support; reduces cough frequency and severity in small clinical trials
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily during acute and chronic bronchitis

items.food: Warm soups — chicken or vegetable broth, rasam, kadhi
items.benefit: Steam from warm soup directly inhales into airways (mini steam inhalation with each sip); hot liquid loosens mucus; chicken broth: cysteine (mucolytic amino acid); sodium; anti-inflammatory N-acetyl cysteine precursors; rasam (South Indian): black pepper, turmeric, tamarind — multiple anti-inflammatory and mucolytic compounds; decongestant effect from vapour; provides nutrition during illness when appetite poor

recommended_foods.category: Anti-Inflammatory Foods (Benefit Chronic Bronchitis and Reduce AECB Frequency)
recommended_foods.rationale: Chronic bronchitis is characterised by persistent neutrophilic and oxidative airway inflammation — anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (Mediterranean diet, DASH diet) have been associated with slower FEV1 decline and reduced COPD exacerbations in large epidemiological studies

items.benefit: Curcumin — most potent natural NF-κB inhibitor (NF-κB drives airway inflammation in COPD); inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis; reduces IL-8, TNF-alpha, MMP-12 (elastase — causes emphysematous tissue destruction); antioxidant; reduces airway hyperresponsiveness; black pepper (piperine) enhances curcumin bioavailability by 20-fold (otherwise very poorly absorbed)
items.frequency: Daily in food; turmeric golden milk (haldi doodh) at bedtime; use with black pepper — both essential

items.food: Fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, hilsa — Ilish)
items.benefit: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) — reduce leukotriene B4 (LTB4 — potent neutrophil chemoattractant in COPD airways); reduce IL-6 and TNF-alpha; improve alveolar macrophage function; epidemiological evidence: high fish consumption associated with slower FEV1 decline and reduced COPD risk; anti-inflammatory prostaglandin E3 production

Polyphenols (quercetin, resveratrol, ellagic acid) — antioxidant, anti-inflammatory; quercetin inhibits histamine release (antihistaminic); resveratrol activates SIRT1 deacetylase (deacetylates and silences inflammatory gene expression — impaired in COPD); amla: richest food source of Vitamin C; reduces airway oxidative stress

items.food: Dark leafy vegetables (palak/spinach, methi, sarson ka saag)
items.benefit: Magnesium (bronchodilatory — IV magnesium sulphate used in acute severe asthma; dietary magnesium associated with better lung function in population studies); folate; Vitamin K; Vitamin C; antioxidants; carotenoids
items.frequency: Daily — integral part of Indian diet already

items.benefit: Allicin, quercetin, thiosulfinates — anti-inflammatory, antiviral, antibacterial; garlic reduces susceptibility to common cold (Cochrane: garlic reduces cold incidence); quercetin in onion inhibits histamine release; flavonoids reduce airway hyperresponsiveness

recommended_foods.category: High-Antioxidant Foods (Protect Against Oxidative Damage in COPD)
recommended_foods.rationale: Cigarette smoke and chronic airway inflammation generate massive oxidative stress in COPD airways — the antioxidant defence system (glutathione, superoxide dismutase, catalase) is overwhelmed; dietary antioxidants supplement these defences

items.food: Amla (Indian Gooseberry) — the supreme Indian antioxidant food
items.benefit: 600-900 mg Vitamin C per 100g (the highest Vitamin C food); tannins, gallic acid, ellagic acid (powerful antioxidants); Emblicanin A and B (potent free radical scavengers); enhances natural killer cell activity; regenerates Vitamin E (synergistic antioxidant pair); clinical trials show amla reduces oxidative stress markers in respiratory disease
items.frequency: 1-2 amla daily; amla murabba, raw, or juice (diluted)

items.food: Vitamin C-rich foods (guava, papaya, kiwi, citrus)
items.benefit: Vitamin C is the primary aqueous antioxidant in respiratory tract lining fluid; deficiency associated with worse COPD outcomes; low Vitamin C intake associated with higher FEV1 decline in large cohort studies; 200 mg/day from food is achievable and associated with optimal lung function

items.food: Nuts and seeds (almonds, walnuts, sunflower seeds)
items.benefit: Vitamin E (fat-soluble antioxidant — protects cell membranes from lipid peroxidation); selenium (deiodinase cofactor AND glutathione peroxidase cofactor — antioxidant); magnesium (bronchodilatory); healthy fats (anti-inflammatory); protein (supports respiratory muscle mass in COPD); high energy density for COPD cachexia
items.frequency: Daily handful as snack — particularly important in COPD for energy density

recommended_foods.category: High-Energy, High-Protein Foods — Critical in COPD Cachexia
recommended_foods.rationale: COPD cachexia (involuntary weight loss) affects up to 40% of COPD patients; low BMI (<18.5) is an independent predictor of mortality in COPD; increased respiratory work of breathing raises resting energy expenditure by 15-25%; dyspnoea reduces appetite and meal size (breathless while eating); malnutrition worsens respiratory muscle weakness — creating a vicious cycle

items.benefit: High-quality complete protein; calcium; phosphorus; casein (slow-release protein — ideal for maintaining positive nitrogen balance overnight); high energy density; soft and easy to eat without excessive dyspnoea
items.frequency: Daily in COPD patients with low BMI

items.benefit: Complete protein (all essential amino acids); leucine (key trigger for muscle protein synthesis — prevents muscle wasting); Vitamin D; selenium; B12; easy to prepare and eat; versatile

items.food: Mung beans and lentils (moong dal, masoor)
items.benefit: Plant protein; B vitamins; potassium; magnesium; antioxidants; low glycaemic index (avoids CO2 spike from rapid carbohydrate metabolism); soft and easy to eat; economical
items.frequency: Daily as dal in Indian diet

items.benefit: Monounsaturated fatty acids (anti-inflammatory); very high energy density (high fat — important for COPD energy needs); low carbohydrate (reduces CO2 production from metabolism); potassium; folate; Vitamin E
items.frequency: 3-4 times per week in COPD cachexia — excellent calorie-dense food

recommended_foods.category: Low-Carbohydrate, Higher-Fat Dietary Approach (for CO2 Retainers)
recommended_foods.rationale: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the metabolic byproduct of carbohydrate and fat oxidation. Carbohydrates generate MORE CO2 per oxygen consumed (respiratory quotient RQ = 1.0) compared to fats (RQ = 0.7). In patients with chronic CO2 retention (type 2 respiratory failure in severe COPD), a high-carbohydrate diet increases CO2 production, worsening hypercapnia. A lower-carbohydrate, higher-fat diet reduces CO2 load and may improve gas exchange.
practical_advice: Replace large portions of rice, bread, and potatoes with higher-fat alternatives (olive oil, nuts, avocado, full-fat dairy) in severe hypercapnic COPD
Small frequent meals (5-6 per day instead of 3 large) — large meals elevate diaphragm, causing worsening breathlessness in COPD; small meals avoid post-meal dyspnoea
Main protein source: lean meat, fish, eggs, paneer — lower carbohydrate, adequate protein
Consult dietitian for severe malnutrition or severe COPD — individualised dietary plan

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Excessive Dairy Products (Acute Bronchitis — Traditional Advice)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Traditional belief that dairy thickens mucus is partly supported: casomorphin (a peptide from casein in cow's milk) may increase mucus production in some individuals; milk may increase perceived mucus thickness; however, evidence is not universal — if dairy does not worsen symptoms for an individual, no need to restrict.
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Reduce cold dairy (cold milk, ice cream) during acute bronchitis if it seems to worsen mucus or cough; warmed milk with turmeric (haldi doodh) is tolerable for most; yogurt (probiotic) is generally beneficial and does not worsen mucus

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Cold air and cold beverages trigger airway hyperresponsiveness and bronchospasm in bronchitis — cold receptors in the larynx and trachea trigger cough reflex and bronchospasm; cold liquids also suppress mucociliary function temporarily
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Prefer warm or room-temperature beverages during acute illness; avoid cold drinks from refrigerator; avoid ice cream during bronchitis

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Cigarettes, Bidis, and All Tobacco Products
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: The most important dietary and lifestyle avoidance in bronchitis — smoking is the primary cause of chronic bronchitis and the most important preventable factor worsening all forms of bronchitis. Even one cigarette acutely increases airway resistance, impairs mucociliary clearance, and triggers bronchospasm. Each cigarette smoked during acute bronchitis prolongs illness and recovery.
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: STOP SMOKING COMPLETELY — this is the single most important intervention; use combination NRT + behavioral support + varenicline if needed; every GP appointment for bronchitis is an opportunity for cessation counselling (ABC approach: Ask, Brief advice, Cessation support)

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Trans fats and saturated fats promote systemic and airway inflammation (increase IL-6, CRP, and NF-κB activity); contribute to obesity which worsens breathlessness (abdominal fat restricts diaphragm descent); processed foods often high in sodium (water retention worsens airway oedema)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Replace with olive oil, mustard oil, or ghee in moderation; bake or steam rather than deep-fry

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Alcohol impairs mucociliary function (reduces ciliary beat frequency — essential for clearing bronchial mucus); impairs alveolar macrophage function (reduces bacterial killing); dehydrating (worsens mucus viscosity); interacts with many bronchitis medications (theophylline clearance altered; respiratory depression with sedatives); worsens GORD (reflux-related cough)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Reduce or eliminate alcohol during acute illness; moderate consumption (within guidelines) in chronic stable COPD; avoid completely if on sedatives or theophylline

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: High dietary sodium promotes airway hyperresponsiveness in susceptible individuals; contributes to systemic hypertension and fluid retention (worsens cor pulmonale oedema in COPD); high-sodium processed foods also contain preservatives that may trigger bronchospasm in sensitive patients (sulfites in wine and dried fruits)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Reduce processed food and added salt; use iodised salt in moderation in cooking

steam_inhalation.description: A widely used traditional and medically-endorsed home treatment for bronchitis — inhaling steam from hot water directly into the airways
steam_inhalation.benefit: Hydrates and warms dry inflamed airways; loosens thick tenacious mucus making it easier to cough up; temporary relief of nasal congestion; adding eucalyptus oil (nilgiri tel) or Vicks VapoRub provides additional menthol-mediated cooling sensation and mild decongestant effect; the sense of relief is significant for patient comfort
steam_inhalation.method: Fill bowl with very hot (not boiling) water; optionally add 2-5 drops of eucalyptus essential oil or ½ teaspoon ajwain (carom seeds); drape towel over head and bowl creating a tent; breathe in steam slowly and deeply for 5-10 minutes; repeat 2-3 times daily
steam_inhalation.cautions: Severe burn risk in children under 5 years — DO NOT USE steam inhalation in young children; use cool-mist humidifier instead; never use boiling water; never use in asthmatics (steam may trigger bronchospasm in some)

acute_bronchitis.principle: Easy to eat, immune-supporting, warm, hydrating foods; avoid cold, fried, and mucus-thickening foods
acute_bronchitis.morning: Warm water with honey and lemon (on waking); adrak-tulsi chai (ginger-holy basil tea); 1-2 amla (whole or juice)
acute_bronchitis.breakfast: Moong dal khichdi with minimal spice and a little ghee; OR plain daliya (broken wheat porridge); OR soft idli with thin sambar (no heavy chutney); avoid cold milk and cereal
acute_bronchitis.mid_morning: Warm turmeric milk (haldi doodh) with black pepper and ginger; ripe banana
acute_bronchitis.lunch: Chicken or vegetable rasam (South Indian — pepper, tamarind, tomato — excellent expectorant and bronchodilator); plain steamed rice; boiled egg; dal
acute_bronchitis.afternoon: Steam inhalation (5-10 minutes); ginger tea with honey
acute_bronchitis.dinner: Clear chicken broth; khichdi or soft rice with dal; steamed vegetables; NO cold drinks, ice cream, or fried food
acute_bronchitis.bedtime: Warm haldi doodh (turmeric milk); 1 teaspoon honey

chronic_bronchitis_copd.principle: High energy (for cachexia prevention), anti-inflammatory, small frequent meals, adequate protein
chronic_bronchitis_copd.early_morning: Warm water; 1-2 walnuts and almonds (Vitamin E, omega-3, energy)
chronic_bronchitis_copd.breakfast: Eggs (scrambled or boiled) with whole wheat toast and avocado/butter; or moong dal chilla (protein-rich pancake); small cup of tea (not too strong)
chronic_bronchitis_copd.mid_morning: Amla murabba (1-2); handful mixed seeds (pumpkin, sunflower); coconut water
chronic_bronchitis_copd.lunch: Fish curry (salmon or mackerel — omega-3) or chicken; dal; brown rice or 1-2 roti; cooked vegetables with haldi; curd (probiotic)
chronic_bronchitis_copd.afternoon: Paneer cubes or nuts; ginger tea
chronic_bronchitis_copd.dinner: Lighter meal — moong dal soup; vegetable khichdi; boiled vegetables; do NOT eat large heavy meal (worsens dyspnoea from stomach distension)
chronic_bronchitis_copd.bedtime: Warm haldi doodh; avoid heavy food within 2-3 hours of sleep (GORD worsens cough)

smoking_cessation.overview: The single most important lifestyle intervention — in chronic bronchitis, smoking cessation at ANY stage of disease halves the annual rate of FEV1 decline. In acute bronchitis, continuing to smoke dramatically prolongs illness duration and increases the risk of developing COPD with repeated infections. Smoking cessation is the ONLY intervention proven to reduce long-term mortality in COPD.

brief_advice_abc.A: ASK — Ask about smoking at every clinical encounter ('Do you currently smoke?')
brief_advice_abc.B: BRIEF ADVICE — Give personalised, non-judgmental brief advice ('The most important thing for your breathing is to stop smoking — can we discuss how I can help?')
brief_advice_abc.C: CESSATION SUPPORT — Offer referral to stop smoking service; prescribe NRT, varenicline, or bupropion; arrange follow-up; celebrate successes

practical_strategies: Set a definite quit date — within 2 weeks of making the decision; do NOT taper (cold turkey with medication support is more effective than gradual reduction without medication)
Combination approach most effective: medication (varenicline or combination NRT) + behavioural support (counselling, apps, support group) doubles quit rates over medication alone
Identify triggers and high-risk situations — develop specific plans for each trigger (tea break: replace cigarette with walk; alcohol: avoid for first month; stress: alternative coping strategy)
Remove all tobacco products and ashtrays from home, car, and workplace
Ask family members and housemates to support quit attempt — ideally quit together
iQuit (India): free government cessation helpline and app; NCDC quit tobacco programme
Avoid situations with heavy smokers (parties, certain social contexts) for first 2-3 months — strongest cravings in first weeks; 'delay-distract-deep-breathe' technique for urges
Physical activity reduces cravings (5-minute walk reduces cigarette craving intensity for 50 minutes — 'the 5-minute rule')

air_quality_and_pollution.overview: Air quality profoundly affects both acute bronchitis frequency and chronic bronchitis progression — particularly in India with the world's highest levels of outdoor air pollution in many cities. Practical steps to reduce pollution exposure:
indoor_measures: Replace biomass cooking fuels (wood, dung, coal, crop residue) with LPG, piped gas, or electric cooking — the Indian government Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana scheme provides subsidised LPG connections; this SINGLE change can halve COPD risk in rural women
Ensure adequate kitchen ventilation — extractor fan or cross-ventilation; cook with doors and windows open whenever possible

Install HEPA air purifier in bedroom (where most time is spent sleeping) — removes PM2.5, PM10, and allergens; HEPA-grade filters remove >99.97% of particles >0.3 microns; most important investment for COPD patients in polluted Indian cities
Avoid incense sticks (agarbatti), mosquito coils, and room freshener sprays indoors — these are significant sources of indoor PM2.5 and VOCs that worsen bronchitis
Ban smoking inside the home — second-hand smoke causes bronchitis in children and non-smoking family members; even one smoker indoors significantly worsens COPD in cohabitants
Regular damp dusting and vacuuming (HEPA vacuum) to reduce house dust mite allergen
outdoor_measures: Monitor local AQI (Air Quality Index) daily — use apps like Safar-Air, IQAir, or CPCB Sameer app (India); reduce outdoor activity on high-pollution days (AQI >150)
Schedule outdoor exercise and activities in early morning (before traffic peak — lower PM2.5) or in parks away from main roads

Use N95 respirator masks when outdoors in high-pollution conditions (Delhi winter smog, crop burning season October-November) — N95 filters 95% of PM2.5; surgical masks provide minimal PM2.5 protection
Keep car windows closed in heavy traffic; use car air recirculation setting (NOT fresh air intake) in traffic jams — this reduces interior PM2.5 by up to 75%
Ensure vaccinations are current — influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations reduce severity of pollution-triggered exacerbations

pulmonary_rehabilitation.overview: Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) is one of the most evidence-based and cost-effective interventions for COPD — a structured exercise training programme combined with education and psychosocial support. PR is not available in all centres in India but is expanding rapidly.
components: Aerobic exercise training — walking, cycling, swimming, treadmill; intensity at 60-80% of maximum; typically 3-5 sessions per week for 6-8 weeks minimum
Resistance training — upper and lower limb exercises to reverse peripheral muscle deconditioning (skeletal muscle dysfunction is a major systemic manifestation of COPD)
Breathing retraining — pursed-lip breathing (slows expiration, prevents dynamic airway collapse); diaphragmatic breathing technique

Airway clearance techniques — Active Cycle of Breathing (ACBT): breathing control → thoracic expansion exercises → forced expiration technique (huff coughing); postural drainage (gravity-assisted drainage for productive bronchitis with large sputum volumes)

Education — disease understanding; inhaler technique assessment and correction (majority of COPD patients use inhalers incorrectly); smoking cessation reinforcement; exacerbation action plan; advance care planning for severe disease
pulmonary_rehabilitation.evidence: Multiple Cochrane reviews: PR reduces dyspnoea, increases exercise capacity (6-minute walk test +50-100 metres), improves quality of life (SGRQ score), reduces hospitalisation for AECB by 33%, and reduces post-exacerbation re-hospitalisation by 50%. Effects persist for 12-24 months post-programme. Early PR within 4 weeks post-AECB hospitalisation is now strongly recommended.
home_exercise_programme: Brisk walking: start with 5-10 minutes twice daily; increase by 5 minutes per week; target 30 minutes most days
Cycling (static or outdoor): excellent aerobic exercise with less lower limb impact; suitable for moderate-severe COPD
Arm exercises (shoulder raises, arm circles) — strengthen accessory muscles of respiration
Sit-to-stand exercises — strengthens quadriceps (major muscle wasting in COPD)

Yoga: Pranayama (breathing exercises) — anulom vilom, bhramari, kapalbhati (modified gentle version for COPD); stretching improves thoracic mobility; evidence for yoga improving quality of life in COPD

pursed_lip_breathing.description: Breathe in slowly through nose for 2 counts; purse lips as if about to blow out a candle; breathe out slowly through pursed lips for 4 counts (twice as long as inhalation)
pursed_lip_breathing.benefit: Slows respiratory rate; increases expiratory time; creates back-pressure that splints small airways open preventing dynamic collapse during expiration; reduces air trapping and hyperinflation; reduces sense of breathlessness; can be done anywhere during dyspnoea episodes
pursed_lip_breathing.evidence: Reduces dyspnoea score significantly; improves oxygen saturation during exercise in COPD

diaphragmatic_breathing.description: Lying on back with knees bent; place one hand on chest and one on abdomen; breathe in through nose — abdomen should rise (not chest); breathe out through pursed lips — abdomen falls; practice 5-10 minutes twice daily
diaphragmatic_breathing.benefit: Retrains respiratory pattern to use diaphragm (most efficient respiratory muscle) rather than accessory muscles; reduces oxygen cost of breathing; improves gas exchange

active_cycle_of_breathing.description: (1) Breathing control: gentle relaxed breathing for 1 minute; (2) Thoracic expansion: 3-4 deep slow breaths with 3-second pause at peak inspiration (helps gas distribution); (3) Forced expiration technique (FET / huffing): gentle medium-volume huff — keep mouth and glottis open, contract abdominal muscles to force air out (as if trying to steam up glasses); much more effective and less bronchospasm-inducing than hard coughing
active_cycle_of_breathing.benefit: Clears mucus from airways without causing bronchospasm or exhaustion; superior to coughing for clearing lower respiratory secretions; particularly valuable in chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis with large daily sputum volumes

infection_prevention_and_exacerbation_ma.AECB_action_plan: All COPD patients should have a personalised written exacerbation action plan: recognise early symptoms of AECB (increased dyspnoea, cough, sputum colour change); keep rescue salbutamol inhaler at home; keep pre-prescribed 'rescue pack' of oral prednisolone 30 mg × 5 days + appropriate antibiotic (doxycycline or amoxicillin); know when to call doctor; know emergency signs requiring immediate hospital attendance
infection_prevention_and_exacerbation_ma.hand_hygiene: Regular handwashing with soap for 20 seconds — respiratory viruses spread by hand-to-mucous membrane contact; hand sanitiser (>60% alcohol) when soap unavailable
infection_prevention_and_exacerbation_ma.respiratory_hygiene: Cover mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing (elbow not hand); dispose of used tissues immediately; avoid close contact with people who have colds or respiratory infections
infection_prevention_and_exacerbation_ma.vaccination: Annual influenza vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine are the most important preventive measures for AECB and bronchitis in at-risk patients
infection_prevention_and_exacerbation_ma.sleep_position: Sleep with head elevated (2-3 pillows or head of bed raised) — reduces nocturnal GORD and post-nasal drip (both worsen cough); also reduces nocturnal bronchospasm from acid aspiration

bronchitis_monitoring_plan.note: Monitoring plan varies dramatically between acute bronchitis (short-term, self-limiting) and chronic bronchitis/COPD (lifelong monitoring). Most acute bronchitis resolves without medical intervention. Chronic bronchitis requires regular scheduled follow-up to monitor progression, optimise therapy, and prevent exacerbations.

green_zone.criteria: Cough improving (though may still be present); temperature returning to normal; no difficulty breathing; able to eat and drink normally; sputum volume reducing; general wellbeing improving
green_zone.action: Continue supportive home care (fluids, honey, steam, paracetamol for fever); no antibiotics needed; reassure that cough may persist up to 3 weeks — this is NORMAL; return to work when fever-free and feeling well enough

yellow_zone.status: GP or Urgent Care Review Required
yellow_zone.criteria: Cough not improving after 7-10 days; fever not resolving; new breathlessness; coughing producing blood; returning or worsening symptoms after initial improvement; known COPD or asthma with worsening symptoms; high-risk individual (elderly, immunocompromised, known lung disease)
yellow_zone.action: Same-day GP review; chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia; consider antibiotics if features of bacterial infection or high-risk patient; spirometry if underlying COPD or asthma suspected

red_zone.status: Emergency Department or Call Emergency Services
criteria: Difficulty breathing at rest; respiratory rate >25/min
High fever >39°C with chest signs not responding to home care
Known COPD patient with severe worsening dyspnoea, confusion, or cyanosis
Infant with bronchiolitis showing respiratory distress (intercostal recession, nasal flaring, grunting)

routine_monitoring: Spirometry: baseline at diagnosis; annually to monitor FEV1 decline; after smoking cessation to demonstrate benefit
Pulse oximetry: at every appointment; SpO2 <92% at rest = assess for long-term oxygen therapy
Exacerbation frequency: document number of AECB per year; >2 per year = step up therapy; consider prophylactic azithromycin or roflumilast
Inhaler technique assessment: at every appointment — majority of patients have sub-optimal technique; recorrect each visit
Smoking status: document and actively support cessation at every consultation
COPD Assessment Test (CAT score) or mMRC dyspnoea scale: quantify symptom burden at each visit
6-minute walk test: annually in moderate-severe COPD — declines in distance predict hospitalisation and mortality
Body weight and BMI: quarterly in moderate-severe COPD — weight loss is a poor prognostic sign
Annual chest X-ray: baseline and when significant change in condition; not routine annual unless indicated
Blood eosinophil count: guides ICS use in COPD (eosinophils ≥300/mcL benefit most from ICS addition)
ECG: annually in severe COPD (cor pulmonale, arrhythmia screening)

complications.description: The most feared and common serious complication of acute bronchitis — bacterial superinfection descends from the bronchi into the alveoli causing lobar or bronchopneumonia. The same viruses causing bronchitis (influenza, RSV, adenovirus) damage bronchial epithelium and impair mucociliary clearance, allowing bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae) to colonise and infect the alveoli. Pneumonia presents with higher fever, pleuritic chest pain, focal crackles, and CXR consolidation — distinguishing it from bronchitis.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — requires specific antibiotic treatment; can be life-threatening in elderly, COPD, and immunocompromised
complications.risk_factors_for_progression: Age >65, COPD, diabetes, immunosuppression, smoking, alcoholism, aspiration risk
complications.management: Antibiotics (amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, or macrolide/tetracycline for atypicals); CURB-65 score for hospitalisation decision; oxygen if SpO2 <94%; IV antibiotics and hospital admission for severe cases

complications.complication: COPD Development from Recurrent Acute Bronchitis
complications.description: Repeated episodes of acute bronchitis — particularly in smokers — cause cumulative irreversible remodelling of the airways. Each episode accelerates the progression from normal lung function through subclinical small airway disease to measurable COPD. Viral bronchitis in childhood (particularly RSV bronchiolitis, adenovirus) permanently impairs airway development, lowering the peak FEV1 attained — such individuals reach the COPD threshold much earlier than those with normal airway development.
complications.management: Smoking cessation; pneumococcal and influenza vaccination to reduce AECB frequency; spirometry in all adults with recurrent bronchitis and smoking history to detect early COPD

complications.description: Chronic hypoxia from advanced COPD/chronic bronchitis causes pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction → elevated pulmonary arterial pressure (pulmonary hypertension) → progressive right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation → right heart failure (cor pulmonale). Presents with ankle oedema, raised JVP, hepatomegaly, and worsening dyspnoea. ECG: P pulmonale, right axis deviation, right bundle branch block. CXR: enlarged pulmonary arteries.
complications.severity: Severe — significantly worsens COPD prognosis; median survival after diagnosis of cor pulmonale is 2-3 years
complications.management: Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT — >15 hours per day at home) is the only treatment proven to reduce pulmonary hypertension and improve survival in cor pulmonale; diuretics for oedema; optimise COPD management; smoking cessation

complications.description: Type 1 (hypoxic — low PaO2, normal/low PaCO2) or Type 2 (hypercapnic — low PaO2 + high PaCO2) respiratory failure from severe AECB. Occurs when the respiratory muscles can no longer sustain adequate gas exchange despite maximum effort. Type 2 respiratory failure with CO2 narcosis (rising PaCO2 causes progressive sedation, confusion, and eventually coma) is particularly dangerous.
complications.management: Controlled oxygen (SpO2 88-92% in COPD); NIV (BiPAP) for pH <7.35; invasive mechanical ventilation if NIV fails; ICU

complications.description: Transient airway hyperresponsiveness (increased sensitivity to bronchospasm triggers) persisting for weeks to months after viral bronchitis — even in individuals with no prior history of asthma. Known as 'post-infectious bronchial hyperresponsiveness' or 'cough-variant asthma'. Manifests as: persistent wheeze; episodic dyspnoea from minor triggers; prolonged cough beyond expected resolution. A small proportion of these individuals develop permanent asthma.
complications.management: Short-acting bronchodilator (salbutamol inhaler) for bronchospasm episodes; short course ICS if severe and prolonged; spirometry with bronchodilator test; reassurance that it usually resolves within 6-8 weeks; review if persisting >3 months

complications.description: Permanent abnormal dilation of the bronchi (bronchiectasis) from recurrent severe respiratory infections that destroy bronchial wall integrity. Particularly associated with: untreated pertussis, severe measles-related pneumonia, recurrent aspiration, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immune deficiency. Chronic productive cough with large volumes of purulent sputum (>30 mL/day), recurrent pneumonias, and haemoptysis are characteristic. HRCT shows characteristic 'signet ring sign' (bronchus wider than adjacent artery).
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — progressive; reduces life expectancy if severe
complications.management: Airway clearance techniques (ACBT, Flutter device, Acapella); physiotherapy; antibiotics for exacerbations (guided by sputum culture — often Pseudomonas); long-term azithromycin prophylaxis; pulmonary rehabilitation; surgery (resection) for localised severe bronchiectasis

complications.description: Untreated or severe Bordetella pertussis infection can cause: pneumonia (secondary bacterial, particularly fatal in infants); hypoxic seizures from coughing bouts causing transient hypoxia; apnoea (breathing pauses — leading cause of pertussis death in infants); subconjunctival haemorrhage (from raised intracranial pressure during coughing paroxysms); rib fractures (from severe coughing in adults); urinary incontinence (stress from coughing); syncope (post-tussive).
complications.management: Azithromycin early; supportive care; hospital admission for infants, severely ill adults, or complications; isolate; notify public health

complications.complication: COPD Cachexia and Skeletal Muscle Dysfunction
complications.description: Progressive involuntary weight loss and muscle wasting (sarcopenia) affecting up to 40% of COPD patients — a systemic manifestation of chronic inflammation, physical inactivity, oxidative stress, and hypoxia. Skeletal muscle wasting is an independent predictor of mortality in COPD, exercise intolerance, and impaired quality of life. Low BMI (<21) is associated with a 2-3 fold increase in COPD mortality.
complications.management: Nutritional assessment and support (dietitian referral); high-protein, energy-dense diet; pulmonary rehabilitation (resistance training rebuilds muscle mass); anabolic hormones (testosterone supplementation in deficient males with COPD — under specialist supervision); nutritional supplementation

key_points: Acute bronchitis is extremely common in children — average 6-8 respiratory infections per year in preschool children; most are viral and self-limiting

RSV bronchiolitis (inflammation of small bronchioles — bronchioles not bronchi) is distinct from adult bronchitis: affects infants under 2 years; clinical features: wheeze, tachypnoea, intercostal recession, hyperinflation; managed supportively (oxygen, NG feeds, hydration); no evidence for bronchodilators, steroids, or antibiotics in most cases

Pertussis (whooping cough) is particularly dangerous in infants — can cause fatal apnoea; treat ALL suspected pertussis with azithromycin; report to public health; ensure household contacts vaccinated

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis — usually parainfluenza virus): barking 'seal-like' cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarse voice; treat with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; nebulised adrenaline for severe stridor; steroids reduce severity significantly
Antibiotics for acute bronchitis in children: NOT indicated for viral bronchitis; DO NOT prescribe without a specific reason (pertussis, Mycoplasma, or bacterial pneumonia)

Honey for cough: highly effective and safe in children over 12 months (NOT under 12 months — infant botulism risk); 1 teaspoon honey at bedtime reduces nocturnal cough comparably to dextromethorphan (RCT evidence)

Recurrent bronchitis in children: always investigate for: asthma (most common cause of recurrent cough — reversible wheeze on spirometry), cystic fibrosis (sweat test), immune deficiency, VUR and recurrent aspiration, and pertussis

Passive smoking: children in smoking households have 2-3 times higher bronchitis and respiratory infection rates; 'smoke-free home' advice is mandatory when a child is repeatedly presenting with bronchitis

Elderly patients are at significantly higher risk of acute bronchitis progressing to pneumonia — impaired mucociliary clearance, decreased cough strength, reduced immunological reserves, and multiple comorbidities
COPD prevalence dramatically increases with age — over 20% of adults over 75 have COPD; often undiagnosed until an exacerbation or pneumonia occurs
Influenza in the elderly causes disproportionate mortality — annual influenza vaccination is critical; antiviral therapy (oseltamivir) should be given promptly in high-risk elderly with influenza

ACE inhibitor-related cough is very common in elderly (up to 15% of users) — always check medications in any elderly patient presenting with 'bronchitis'; substitute ARB (valsartan, losartan) if cough is from ACE inhibitor

Multiple medications in the elderly may interfere with bronchitis management: beta-blockers worsen bronchospasm in COPD (avoid non-selective — use cardioselective beta-1 selective agents like bisoprolol if essential); NSAIDs exacerbate heart failure and renal impairment; sedatives must be used with extreme caution (CO2 retention risk)

Inhaler technique: poor manual dexterity, cognitive impairment, and reduced inspiratory flow in elderly impair MDI use — use spacer devices (Aerochamber) with MDI, or switch to breath-actuated inhalers (Autohaler, Easybreath) or DPI with lower resistance (Respimat, Genuair)

Pneumococcal and influenza vaccination: both are critically important in elderly COPD — reduce AECB frequency and pneumonia risk; influenza vaccine reduces hospitalisation for acute respiratory illness by 40-50% in this age group

Acute viral bronchitis in pregnancy: most cases are uncomplicated viral illness; increased risk of influenza severity (higher ICU admission and mortality in pregnant women); oseltamivir should be given promptly to pregnant women with suspected influenza (safe in all trimesters, risk-benefit clearly favours treatment)

Pertussis in pregnancy: diagnose and treat with azithromycin (safe in pregnancy); critically important for Tdap vaccination in third trimester (27-36 weeks) to protect neonate via passive antibody transfer before infant can be vaccinated

Antibiotics in pregnancy for bronchitis: only if specific indication (pertussis, Mycoplasma, bacterial pneumonia); safe antibiotics: amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, azithromycin, cefalexin; AVOID: fluoroquinolones (fetal cartilage effects — avoid especially first trimester), tetracyclines (fetal bone and tooth development), chloramphenicol (neonatal grey baby syndrome)

Asthma in pregnancy: well-controlled asthma is essential — poorly controlled asthma causes preterm birth, IUGR, and pre-eclampsia; all regular asthma medications (ICS, LABA, salbutamol, montelukast) are safe; do NOT stop ICS in pregnancy (risk of asthma attack > theoretical risk of medication)
Inhalers in pregnancy: all standard bronchodilators and ICS are safe and should be continued; inhaled route means minimal systemic drug delivery to fetus
Chest physiotherapy: safe and effective for mucus clearance in chronic productive cough in pregnancy; positioned appropriately to avoid aortocaval compression in supine position

Immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS, post-transplant, chemotherapy, biologics) have impaired ability to fight respiratory infections and are at risk of unusually severe or prolonged bronchitis, unusual organisms, and rapid progression to pneumonia

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) — common in HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200); presents with gradual-onset dyspnoea, dry cough, and minimal chest signs; HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass opacity; treat with high-dose co-trimoxazole; prevent with co-trimoxazole prophylaxis
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis — transplant recipients on immunosuppression; diagnose with CMV PCR and bronchoscopy BAL; treat with IV ganciclovir

Fungal infections — Aspergillus, Cryptococcus in severely immunocompromised; invasive aspergillosis — fever, haemoptysis, pleural rub in neutropenic patients; diagnose with serum galactomannan and HRCT; treat with voriconazole
Lower threshold for hospital admission, chest X-ray, blood cultures, and bronchoscopy (BAL); early empirical antibiotics (including PCP prophylaxis); involve infectious disease specialist early

India has specific high-risk populations for occupational and pollution-related bronchitis: coal miners in Jharkhand and Odisha (pneumoconiosis + bronchitis); brick kiln workers (silica, PM2.5); cotton textile workers in Gujarat and Maharashtra (byssinosis); crop burning season in Punjab, Haryana (October-November — acute severe air quality episodes causing AQI >1000 — hospitalisation spike for respiratory illness)

Biomass fuel cooking — 3 billion people globally including hundreds of millions in India cook on open fires; equivalent exposure to 40+ cigarettes per day; leading cause of COPD in non-smoking Indian rural women (15-40% of COPD in India attributable to biomass fuel); change to LPG under PM Ujjwala Yojana scheme is a priority public health intervention

Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana: free LPG connections for BPL households — transition from biomass to LPG reduces indoor PM2.5 by >70% and is associated with significant reduction in respiratory illness

Occupational health regulations: Factories Act 1948; Mines Act 1952 — require respiratory protective equipment, dust suppression, health surveillance; implementation is variable; chest X-ray every 1-2 years mandatory in high-risk occupations
National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) India: target 20-30% reduction in PM2.5 and PM10 by 2024 in 102 non-attainment cities — public health impact on reducing bronchitis burden

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Once annually before flu season (October-November in India, August-September for maximum immunity; available year-round)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza is the single most common cause of severe acute bronchitis and AECB in COPD patients. Annual vaccination reduces: influenza bronchitis incidence by 50-70%; AECB triggered by influenza by 50%; influenza-related hospitalisations in COPD by 40-50%; influenza-related mortality in elderly COPD patients by 50%. GOLD guidelines: influenza vaccination is the MOST IMPORTANT vaccination for COPD. All patients with chronic bronchitis/COPD, elderly (>65), pregnant women, healthcare workers, and those with asthma should receive annual influenza vaccination.
vaccinations_recommended.effectiveness: 40-70% protective efficacy (varies with vaccine-strain match); significantly reduces severity even when not fully preventive
vaccinations_recommended.recommended_for: All COPD patients; all patients with asthma; all adults >65; pregnant women (all trimesters); immunocompromised patients; healthcare workers; patients with chronic heart, kidney, or liver disease

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PCV15 or PCV20: one-time dose; PPSV23: booster 5 years after first pneumococcal vaccine in high-risk groups
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the most common cause of bacterial pneumonia complicating acute bronchitis and AECB. Pneumococcal vaccination reduces community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) incidence in COPD patients by 24-64% (UK vaccination programme data); significantly reduces severe hospitalisation for respiratory illness. GOLD guidelines: pneumococcal vaccination recommended for all COPD patients.
vaccinations_recommended.recommended_for: All COPD patients; all adults >65; adults with chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease; immunocompromised patients; smokers
vaccinations_recommended.india_note: Pneumococcal vaccination is available privately in India (not routinely included in Universal Immunisation Programme for adults); strongly recommended for all COPD patients; cost approximately Rs 3,000-5,000 per dose

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Pertussis Vaccine (Tdap — Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis Booster)
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Single booster dose (adults); every 10 years with tetanus booster; single dose in each pregnancy (27-36 weeks)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Pertussis immunity from childhood DTP vaccination wanes significantly by adolescence and adulthood — leaving adults susceptible to whooping cough. Adults are an important reservoir for transmission to unvaccinated infants (most vulnerable to fatal pertussis). Pregnant women: Tdap in third trimester (27-36 weeks) provides passive antibody transfer to neonate before infant vaccination is possible — the most effective strategy to protect neonates. Adults with chronic bronchitis: pertussis in COPD can be particularly severe; vaccination reduces risk and population transmission.
vaccinations_recommended.recommended_for: All adults who did not receive Tdap as adolescent; all pregnant women in third trimester; household contacts of newborns (cocooning strategy); healthcare workers; close contacts of COPD patients
vaccinations_recommended.india_note: Tdap (Boostrix, Adacel) available in India; not in national adult immunisation programme but highly recommended

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Primary series and boosters per national schedule
vaccinations_recommended.reason: SARS-CoV-2 causes acute bronchitis ranging from mild to critical; COPD patients have significantly higher risk of severe COVID-19, hospitalisation, mechanical ventilation, and death. COVID-19 is a major trigger for AECB in COPD. Vaccination reduces: COVID-19 severity by 80-90% in vaccinated vs unvaccinated; COVID-19-related AECB; post-COVID persistent respiratory symptoms (Long COVID) — which includes prolonged cough, bronchospasm, and dyspnoea.
vaccinations_recommended.recommended_for: All adults, with priority for: COPD; elderly; immunocompromised; chronic heart, kidney, or liver disease
vaccinations_recommended.india_note: CoWIN platform India; free vaccination available nationally; multiple vaccine options (Covishield, Covaxin, Corbevax)

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: RSV Vaccine / Monoclonal Antibody (emerging — for high-risk populations)
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: RSV vaccines: Abrysvo (Pfizer) and Arexvy (GSK) — approved 2023 for adults >60 years; single dose; may be re-evaluated annually
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is an increasingly recognised major cause of severe acute bronchitis and exacerbations in elderly COPD patients — previously believed to affect only infants. RSV vaccination of adults >60 years and high-risk COPD patients reduces RSV-related LRTI hospitalisation significantly.
vaccinations_recommended.availability: Newly available (2023-2024); availability and regulatory approval in India pending; likely to be incorporated into COPD vaccination recommendations
vaccinations_recommended.nirsevimab: Monoclonal antibody (Beyfortus) for infants — provides RSV passive immunity for one season; highly effective at preventing RSV bronchiolitis hospitalisation; being introduced in high-income countries

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Measles pneumonia and post-measles bronchitis are significant causes of permanent airway damage and bronchiectasis, particularly in children. Measles vaccination is critically important for preventing long-term respiratory complications. India's measles vaccination coverage has improved but outbreaks still occur.
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Ensure all children receive 2 doses of MMR vaccine per national schedule; catch-up vaccination for unvaccinated adolescents and adults without documented measles immunity

when_to_see_doctor: Cough lasting more than 3 weeks without improvement — investigate for pertussis (whooping cough), TB (India — cough >2 weeks + fever/weight loss/night sweats), Mycoplasma, asthma, COPD, GORD, lung cancer
Any blood in sputum (haemoptysis) — however small; always requires chest X-ray minimum; exclude lung cancer, TB, pulmonary embolism, bronchiectasis
Fever above 39°C with cough and breathlessness — chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia
Significant breathlessness — dyspnoea on minimal exertion or at rest is NOT normal with simple bronchitis; investigate for pneumonia, AECB, or new COPD
Oxygen saturation below 94% on pulse oximeter — requires medical assessment same day
Wheeze not resolving after 6-8 weeks following acute bronchitis — spirometry and assessment for asthma or COPD
Recurrent bronchitis (3+ episodes per year) — investigate for underlying asthma, COPD, immunodeficiency, structural lung disease, or TB
New dry cough in a patient on ACE inhibitor (ramipril, enalapril, lisinopril, perindopril) — ACE-inhibitor cough is very common (10-15%); switch to ARB (losartan, valsartan) under GP supervision
Chronic productive cough ('morning cough') in a smoker or bidi smoker over 40 years — spirometry to screen for COPD; early detection allows meaningful intervention
Child with post-tussive vomiting, paroxysmal coughing fits, or suspected contact with whooping cough — urgent GP assessment for pertussis
COPD patient with any worsening of usual symptoms — increased dyspnoea, increased sputum, change in sputum colour — AECB assessment and treatment
Known COPD patient with SpO2 <92% at rest — assessment for long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT)
Any worsening of chronic respiratory symptoms despite compliance with prescribed inhalers — GP review, inhaler technique assessment, and treatment escalation
emergency_signs: Severe dyspnoea at rest — unable to complete sentences; breathing with visibly laboured effort using neck and shoulder muscles — call emergency services (102/112)
Oxygen saturation below 88% on pulse oximeter — severe hypoxia; emergency oxygen and hospital
Cyanosis — blue lips or blue fingernails — severe oxygen deprivation; EMERGENCY
Confusion, altered consciousness, extreme drowsiness in a COPD patient — possible CO2 retention (type 2 respiratory failure / hypercapnic encephalopathy) — EMERGENCY; call 102/112
Respiratory rate above 30 breaths per minute with obvious breathing effort — impending respiratory failure

COPD patient with known severe disease (GOLD III-IV) with acute worsening — higher threshold for emergency care; do NOT give high-flow oxygen (may worsen CO2 retention) — controlled 24-28% oxygen via Venturi mask; call ambulance
Infant with RSV bronchiolitis showing: respiratory rate >60, severe chest recession (sternum pulling in), grunting, apnoea episodes, poor feeding, cyanosis — PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCY
Large haemoptysis (coughing more than a tablespoon of blood) — emergency, may indicate major airway bleeding from cancer or pulmonary embolism
Sudden severe chest pain with breathlessness — possible pneumothorax (spontaneous or in emphysematous COPD), pulmonary embolism, or myocardial infarction — EMERGENCY

Whooping cough in an infant (<6 months): apnoea (stopping breathing), turning blue during coughing, extreme coughing fits in a very young baby — call emergency services immediately; pertussis in infants under 6 months is potentially fatal

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is bronchitis and is it the same as a chest infection?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Bronchitis literally means inflammation of the bronchial tubes — the airways that carry air to your lungs. The most common cause (90%+) is a viral infection — the same viruses responsible for the common cold and flu infect the lower airways, causing a productive cough, chest tightness, and sometimes wheeze. 'Chest infection' is a lay term that covers both bronchitis (airways infected) and pneumonia (lung tissue infected). The crucial difference: bronchitis does NOT usually require antibiotics (it's viral), while pneumonia almost always does. The key distinguishing feature is that pneumonia typically causes high fever (>39°C), significant breathlessness, focal chest signs (crackle sounds in one area), and shows consolidation on chest X-ray — none of which are features of simple acute bronchitis.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why won't my doctor give me antibiotics for bronchitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Over 90% of acute bronchitis is caused by viruses — and antibiotics have absolutely no effect on viruses. Giving antibiotics for viral bronchitis would be equivalent to treating a bruise with vitamin C — no benefit, but real risks. Multiple large clinical trials have shown that antibiotics for acute bronchitis reduce cough duration by only 6-12 hours at best — while causing significant side effects (diarrhoea, allergic reactions, C. difficile colitis) and driving antibiotic resistance. The yellow or green colour of your sputum does NOT mean you have a bacterial infection — it simply reflects the normal immune response (white blood cells colouring the mucus). The most important treatments are: adequate fluids (minimum 2L daily to thin mucus), honey for the cough, paracetamol for fever, and rest. Antibiotics ARE needed for: whooping cough, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, COPD exacerbations meeting criteria, and immunocompromised patients.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I've had a cough for 4 weeks — is this normal after bronchitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, a cough lasting 3-4 weeks after viral bronchitis is common and does not necessarily mean you need antibiotics or have a serious illness. Viruses cause a state of airway hyperresponsiveness (temporary increased sensitivity of the airway cough receptors) that can persist for 4-8 weeks after the infection has cleared — every minor irritant triggers the cough reflex. Up to 50% of patients still have a cough 3 weeks after acute viral bronchitis. However, a cough lasting more than 4 weeks should be assessed by a doctor to rule out: pertussis (whooping cough — especially if coughing fits with post-tussive vomiting), Mycoplasma, new asthma or COPD, GORD (acid reflux), post-nasal drip, ACE-inhibitor side effect, and in India — ALWAYS tuberculosis (TB) if cough >2 weeks with fever, weight loss, or night sweats.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between acute bronchitis and COPD/chronic bronchitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Acute bronchitis is a short-term (1-3 weeks) infection of the airways, most often viral, affecting otherwise healthy people of all ages. It resolves completely. Chronic bronchitis is an entirely different long-term disease — it is part of COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) and is defined as a productive cough persisting for at least 3 months per year for 2 consecutive years. It is caused by years of breathing tobacco smoke, bidi smoke, biomass cooking fuel (wood/dung chulha), or polluted air. Unlike acute bronchitis, chronic bronchitis causes permanent, irreversible damage to the airways and progressively worsening breathlessness. The most important treatment is stopping smoking or removing the cause — nothing else comes close to this in benefit. Inhalers (bronchodilators) and vaccinations are also essential.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I use steam inhalation at home for bronchitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — steam inhalation is a safe and effective home remedy for adults with acute bronchitis. Fill a bowl with very hot (not boiling) water; optionally add 2-5 drops of eucalyptus (nilgiri) oil or a pinch of ajwain (carom seeds); drape a towel over your head creating a tent over the bowl; breathe in the steam slowly for 5-10 minutes. The warm moist air directly hydrates inflamed airways, loosens thick mucus, and provides immediate relief of congestion and chest tightness. It can be done 2-3 times daily. IMPORTANT SAFETY WARNING: Never use steam inhalation for children under 5 years old — the hot water and steam can cause serious burns. Use a cool-mist humidifier (which is completely safe) instead for young children. Also avoid steam in patients with severe asthma as steam can occasionally trigger bronchospasm.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do I use an inhaler correctly? I never seem to get the right technique.
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Poor inhaler technique is extremely common — studies show over 70% of patients use their inhalers incorrectly, significantly reducing effectiveness. For a standard pressurised MDI (pump inhaler) with a spacer device (Aerochamber/Volumatic): shake the inhaler; remove caps; attach to spacer; breathe out fully; place spacer mouthpiece in mouth; press the canister once; breathe in SLOWLY and DEEPLY (over 3-5 seconds); hold breath for 10 seconds; breathe out normally; wait 30-60 seconds before second puff. The spacer device is essential — it holds the medication cloud while you breathe in, allowing much better drug delivery than coordinating pressing and breathing simultaneously. Without a spacer, only 10-20% of the dose reaches your lungs; with a spacer, up to 50% does. Ask your doctor or pharmacist to demonstrate proper technique at each visit — it is one of the most impactful interventions in COPD and asthma management.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is biomass cooking (chulha) really as harmful as smoking for lung health?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — exposure to biomass cooking smoke (from burning wood, cow dung, crop residue, or coal on an open chulha) is one of the most serious and underrecognised respiratory health threats in India. The World Health Organization estimates that indoor air pollution from solid fuel cooking kills more than 4 million people annually worldwide — more than TB and malaria combined. Studies from India consistently show that women cooking on biomass chulhas for several hours daily have lung function equivalent to someone who has smoked a pack of cigarettes per day for 20 years. The particulate matter, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in biomass smoke cause: chronic bronchitis, COPD, lung cancer, cardiovascular disease, and stunted lung development in children. Switching to clean cooking fuel (LPG, electric, biogas) can reverse or halt further lung damage. The Indian Government's Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana provides subsidised LPG connections to below-poverty-line households — transitioning families away from biomass cooking is a critical public health priority.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My child has been coughing non-stop in violent fits for 3 weeks and sometimes vomits after coughing. What could this be?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: This description is HIGHLY SUSPICIOUS for whooping cough (pertussis — Bordetella pertussis infection). The paroxysmal coughing fits (sudden, uncontrollable, violent bouts of coughing), particularly with post-tussive vomiting (vomiting at the end of a coughing bout) and possibly a characteristic 'whoop' sound (high-pitched inspiratory sound after the coughing fit), are the classic features of pertussis. Take your child to a doctor immediately. Pertussis requires: specific antibiotic treatment (azithromycin — reduces spread to others); throat/nasopharyngeal swab PCR test for confirmation; notification to public health; all household contacts treated prophylactically; the child must be kept away from infants (who are most at risk of fatal pertussis) until completing 5 days of antibiotics. Check vaccination status — children may need a DTaP booster if due.
